setting.jp: 明日、京都へ行く予定です。
setting.en: I'm scheduled to go to Kyoto tomorrow.

extensions.scene: Asked about the same trip by a friend rather than by the office, you switch to the one that reports intention instead — both are true of one journey, and you pick by which you are being asked about.
extensions.jp: 京都へ行くつもりです。
extensions.en: I intend to go to Kyoto.

extensions.scene: The distinction survives even when the two disagree, which is the useful case: something can sit on the calendar that you have no intention of doing, and something can be fully intended and nowhere in writing.
extensions.jp: 来年、帰る予定です。
extensions.en: Scheduled to go home next year — the calendar's version.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody at the year-end party says your Japanese has changed and you disagree, and then realise on the train home that you understood most of the party. Nothing happened on any particular day. What the sentence has to report is the arrival of a change rather than an event.
setting.jp: 日本語が話せるようになりました。
setting.en: I've become able to speak Japanese.

extensions.scene: You say it about a habit rather than an ability, about the mornings that used to be impossible, and it is the same claim — a new state, arrived at, with no single moment to point to.
extensions.jp: 毎朝早く起きるようになりました。
extensions.en: I've got to where I get up early.

extensions.scene: It runs in the other direction too, and the reverse is the one people forget — a thing you used to do and have stopped doing is the same arrival, arriving negatively.
extensions.jp: たばこを吸わなくなりました。
extensions.en: I've stopped smoking — the change, arriving the other way.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The difference between the person who improved and the person who did not is usually not talent, and at some point you decide to be deliberate about it. This form is the effort rather than the result — the steering, before there is anything to report.
setting.jp: 毎日日本語を話すようにしています。
setting.en: I make a point of speaking Japanese every day.

extensions.scene: You use it about something you are trying to stop rather than start, which takes the negative inside the clause and leaves the steering machinery on the outside completely untouched.
extensions.jp: たばこを吸わないようにしています。
extensions.en: I'm making a point of not smoking.

extensions.scene: Put this lesson beside the last one and you have the entire arc of a habit in two sentences: the trying, and then months later, without any particular day to point at, the arriving.
extensions.jp: 早く起きるようにしています → 早く起きるようになりました
extensions.en: The effort, then the arrival.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: One axis runs through this entire step and it is not really about grammar: did you choose it, or did it come about? Every pair in the step splits on that one question, and Step 9's warming-the-room versus the-room-warmed was the first rung of the very same ladder.
setting.jp: 日本へ行くことにしました。
setting.en: I chose it — する.

extensions.scene: You build the other half about the same trip, as though the office had decided it, and nothing changes except who is holding the steering wheel — which is the only thing this axis measures.
extensions.jp: 日本へ行くことになりました。
extensions.en: It was decided — なる.

extensions.t: Culture bends the grammar here and it is worth knowing before you mis-hear somebody. Announcements often prefer なる even for things that were plainly chosen — 結婚することになりました is the standard wedding announcement, and nobody hears it as an accident. When you hear なる, do not assume nobody chose.
extensions.scene: Somebody announces their own wedding using the it-was-decided form and for a second you almost congratulate them on their bad luck, before the register catches up with what they actually meant.
extensions.jp: 結婚することになりました。
extensions.en: We're getting married — chosen, announced modestly.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A form for a course you want to take, with a box asking what you can do, and a space for it in writing rather than in conversation. You have had the short potential form since Step 10 and it is not wrong here — but written Japanese leans on the longer, flatter version, and this is the register the box is asking for.
setting.jp: 日本語を話すことができます。
setting.en: I can speak Japanese — stated formally.

extensions.scene: You use it about something narrower further down the same form, where the formality is doing real work — a claim about capability on a document that somebody is going to file and keep.
extensions.jp: 漢字を読むことができます。
extensions.en: I can read kanji.

extensions.scene: You try to combine it with the short potential you already know, stacking two ability machines into a single sentence, and the result means nothing at all in any register of the language.
extensions.jp: 話せることができる
extensions.en: Wrong — one ability machine per sentence.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A new colleague arrives and the getting-to-know-you questions start, and half of them are about whether you have ever done a thing rather than when you did it. English uses a tense for this; Japanese uses a whole construction, and the difference is that this one refuses to carry a date.
setting.jp: 日本へ行ったことがあります。
setting.en: I've been to Japan.

extensions.scene: You ask it back about something specific, which is the shape most of this conversation will take for the next twenty minutes — ever, at any point, with no interest in which year.
extensions.jp: すしを食べたことがありますか。
extensions.en: Have you ever eaten sushi?

extensions.scene: Put a date in the sentence and the whole construction becomes wrong, because you have stopped asking about experience and started reporting an event — and the plain past does that job already.
extensions.jp: 去年、日本へ行きました。
extensions.en: Went last year — a WHEN means plain past, not ことがある.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
去年 uses 去, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed.

setting.scene: The medical form asks how often rather than whether, and there is a row of boxes between always and never that you have no vocabulary for. What you need is a way to say that a thing happens sometimes — not habitually, not never, just occasionally enough to be worth writing down.
setting.jp: 朝ごはんを食べないことがあります。
setting.en: Some mornings I skip breakfast.

extensions.scene: The doctor asks about something else in the same shape, and you answer it yourself — the construction reports frequency somewhere between rarely and regularly, which is where most true answers live.
extensions.jp: 時々、日曜日も働くことがあります。
extensions.en: Sometimes I work Sundays too.

extensions.scene: One kana of tense in front separates this from last lesson entirely. Past means ever, across a whole life. Present means sometimes, in an ordinary week. Nothing else in the sentence changes at all.
extensions.jp: 食べたことがある / 食べることがある
extensions.en: Have eaten, ever / sometimes eat.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The end-of-year party, the second one this week, and the walk to the station is being done slowly by everybody. What you want to say is not that you ate a lot but that you ate more than was wise, which is a judgement rather than a measurement and gets its own suffix.
setting.jp: 昨日は食べすぎました。
setting.en: I ate too much yesterday.

extensions.scene: You use it about something that is not food, about the evening rather than the meal, and it attaches to the front half of a verb exactly the same way.
extensions.jp: 昨日は話しすぎました。
extensions.en: I talked too much last night.

extensions.scene: It chains with the regret ending from Step 13 so naturally that the two behave like one word, and in real speech the combination is what you will hear rather than either of them alone.
extensions.jp: テレビを見すぎてしまいました。
extensions.en: Watched too much television, alas.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Two textbooks for the same course, and the section head wants to know which to order for next year. One of them is not harder — it is worse laid out, with handwriting samples nobody can decipher. That distinction is the whole lesson: this pair describes the thing's character, not your ability.
setting.jp: この本は読みやすいです。
setting.en: This book is easy to read.

extensions.scene: You say the opposite about the other one, and notice that the sentence blames the book rather than the reader — which is the point, and is also the tactful way to say it in a meeting.
extensions.jp: この字は読みにくいです。
extensions.en: This handwriting is hard to read.

extensions.scene: The easy-to half sounds exactly like the word for cheap and has nothing whatever to do with it — same sound, unrelated word, and only what it attaches to tells them apart.
extensions.jp: 使いやすい / 安い
extensions.en: Easy to use / cheap — same sound, no relation.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Third time this form has come round and this is the pass where the rule finally becomes sayable. Somebody asks where a colleague is, and the answer uses the same ending you have used for rain falling and for living in a city — three different jobs from one shape, and the verb decides which.
setting.jp: 田中さんは東京に行っています。
setting.en: Tanaka has gone to Tokyo — and is there now.

extensions.scene: You use it about yourself in the middle of doing something, which is the version you met first — and the shape has not changed at all between the two sentences.
extensions.jp: 今、レポートを書いています。
extensions.en: I'm writing the report now.

extensions.scene: The rule, at last, in a form you can say out loud: a verb naming an instant change wears this as a result, and a verb naming an activity wears it as the middle. Knowing which you hold answers it every time.
extensions.jp: 知っています。住んでいます。
extensions.en: Instant-change verbs, worn as results.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You slept through your phone and there are two missed calls and a message from the office. Explaining it needs a stretch of time and something that happened inside that stretch, and Japanese makes you say which of the two you mean with one extra kana.
setting.jp: 寝ている間に、電話がありました。
setting.en: While I slept, a call came.

extensions.scene: You use the other version about the same nap, where the action fills the whole span rather than landing at one point inside it — and the kana comes off.
extensions.jp: 夏休みの間、日本語を勉強しました。
extensions.en: I studied Japanese all through the summer break.

extensions.scene: The main verb has to agree with the choice you made: one-shot events take the kana, span-filling actions do not. It is a promise about how the verb behaves rather than about the length of the time.
extensions.jp: 授業の間、寝ていました。
extensions.en: Slept through the whole lesson — span, so no に.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Two sentences on the same staffroom whiteboard, both with times in them, and they mean opposite things about what happens at that hour. The meeting runs to three. The report has to be in by three. English leans on until for both, and the difference is a deadline.
setting.jp: 五時までに帰ります。
setting.en: I'll be home by five.

extensions.scene: You write the other one for your own row on the board, about something that continues rather than something that completes, and the kana comes off again without anything else changing.
extensions.jp: 三時まで会議があります。
extensions.en: There's a meeting until three.

extensions.scene: The verb test never fails and takes about a second: does the action continue up to the time, or complete by it? Continuing takes the short one, completing takes the long one.
extensions.jp: 三時までにレポートを出します。
extensions.en: I'll hand the report in by three.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A phone call at the exact moment you are putting your shoes on, asking whether you have left yet. There are three honest answers depending on which second you are standing in — about to, in the middle of, just finished — and Japanese has a single frame with three settings for exactly this.
setting.jp: 今、家を出るところです。
setting.en: I'm just about to leave.

extensions.scene: They ring again forty minutes later and the answer has moved two settings along the same frame, which is the only thing about the sentence that changed between the two calls.
extensions.jp: 今、着いたところです。
extensions.en: I've just this second arrived.

extensions.scene: The just-finished setting is strictly this instant, and next lesson's near-synonym is not — which is why one of them can stretch to a month and this one cannot stretch past a minute.
extensions.jp: 今帰ってきたところです。
extensions.en: Just got back — and it can only mean just now.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Six weeks in and somebody at a dinner asks how the Japanese is coming along. Six weeks is not new by the calendar — it is two pay slips and a haircut — but from the inside it is still the first week, and the question deserves the inside answer.
setting.jp: 先月、日本に来たばかりです。
setting.en: I only just came to Japan.

extensions.scene: You use it about the job rather than about the country, which is also a small request folded into a statement about time — be patient with me, I have only just got here.
extensions.jp: 始めたばかりです。
extensions.en: I've only just started.

extensions.scene: This one measures by feel and last lesson's measures by clock. A month can still be this if it still feels fresh; claiming the strict one about last month would simply be false.
extensions.jp: 先月来たばかりです。
extensions.en: Elastic — where たところ could not stretch at all.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A morning that went wrong in a specific way: the alarm, the train, and out of the door with nothing eaten. What the sentence has to report is not a reason for anything but the manner of the going — the same action, minus something that normally belongs in it.
setting.jp: 朝ごはんを食べないで学校へ行きました。
setting.en: I went to school without breakfast.

extensions.scene: You use it about the report you handed in, which was finished and not checked — again a manner rather than an excuse, and the distinction matters to how the sentence lands.
extensions.jp: 読まないで出しました。
extensions.en: I handed it in without reading it.

extensions.scene: Written Japanese swaps in a shorter form that means exactly the same thing in formal dress. Worth recognising now on documents and notices, and worth producing yourself considerably later on.
extensions.jp: 食べずに
extensions.en: Same meaning, written register — 〜ずに.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The trap is real and it is not subtle once you see it: English leans on until for two things Japanese keeps apart. One is a stretch the action fills. The other is a deadline the action has to beat. Getting them the wrong way round tells your section head something untrue about when the work will exist.
setting.jp: 三時まで会議があります。
setting.en: The meeting RUNS until three.

extensions.scene: You write the deadline version yourself for the thing you owe her by Friday, and the whole difference between the two rows on the board turns out to be one kana that converts a duration into a due date.
extensions.jp: 三時までにレポートを出します。
extensions.en: I'll hand the report in by three.

extensions.t: The fix is the verb test, every time, and it takes a second. Does the action CONTINUE up to that time, or COMPLETE by it? Continuing takes まで. Completing takes までに. Nothing about the time itself decides it.
extensions.scene: You check both sentences on the board against the test and they sort themselves immediately, which is the point — the rule is mechanical once you ask the right question.
extensions.jp: 五時まで待ちます。五時までに帰ります。
extensions.en: I'll wait until five. I'll be home by five.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 20 · Doing to & being done to

setting.scene: A parent describing the evening routine at a parents' evening, and half of it is about getting a nine-year-old to do things he has no intention of doing. English uses make and let and keeps them apart; Japanese uses one form for both and lets the situation decide which you meant.
setting.jp: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。
setting.en: Mum made my brother eat his vegetables.

extensions.scene: You use the letting half yourself, about a child who wanted to finish something after the bell had gone, and it is the same conjugation carrying the opposite social weight entirely.
extensions.jp: 子どもに歌を歌わせました。
extensions.en: I let the children sing.

extensions.scene: Hidden inside this form is the most useful polite request you will learn all year — asking permission by making yourself the person who is being allowed to do the thing.
extensions.jp: すみません、今日は早く帰らせてください。
extensions.en: Sorry — please let me leave early today.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 20 · Doing to & being done to

setting.scene: Half past one, and your class is cleaning the corridor they walk down every day — brooms, cloths, fifteen minutes of it, in the timetable rather than beside it. You say something about it to the teacher next to you, who is old enough to have done it himself for twelve years, and he laughs before he answers.
setting.jp: 毎日、そうじをさせられました。
setting.en: I was made to do the cleaning every day.

extensions.scene: You tell him about your own school in return, about an instrument nobody chose to play, and the form carries the grievance without a single word of complaint anywhere in the sentence.
extensions.jp: 毎日、漢字を書かせられました。
extensions.en: I was made to write kanji every day.

extensions.scene: Two moves, in strict order — causative first, then passive — and speech contracts the long ones, so what you actually hear across a table is shorter than what you learn to build.
extensions.jp: 飲まされました。
extensions.en: Made to drink — the contracted form you'll hear.

claims: A daily cleaning slot of roughly 15-30 minutes, usually after lunch, is standard in Japanese schools
Cleaning appears in the national curriculum standards (学習指導要領), not as an extracurricular add-on
CORRECTS A COMMON CLAIM: Japanese schools do employ caretaking staff (用務員) — 'Japanese schools have no janitors' is wrong
flags: Lloyd teaches in a Japanese school and is the best available check on this one.
The 用務員 correction lives only in claims[] — it did not fit the setting at 45-80 words. If it should be visible to the learner it needs its own sentence.

items.step: Step 20 · Doing to & being done to

setting.scene: Sports day, and the entire field is shouting one word at a child running the last hundred metres. It is a bare command, the rudest form in the language, and nobody within a kilometre thinks it is rude — because cheering suspends the rudeness completely, which is the only everyday place it does.
setting.jp: がんばれ！
setting.en: Go on! You've got this!

extensions.scene: You shout it yourself, which is the one time all year you will produce this form on purpose, and then you spend the rest of the year only recognising it.
extensions.jp: 見て！
extensions.en: Look! — the softer everyday alternative.

extensions.scene: Production is rare and recognition is constant: signs, sports, fiction. Characters bark it at each other for dramatic reasons that do not transfer to a staffroom on an ordinary Tuesday.
extensions.jp: 止まれ
extensions.en: STOP — on a sign, where it belongs.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 20 · Doing to & being done to

setting.scene: The imperative you will actually meet in print, on every worksheet and every exam paper in the building, and on nobody's lips except a parent's. From a question sheet it is neutral instruction. Aimed sideways at an adult it is parenting them, and it lands exactly that way.
setting.jp: 早く寝なさい。
setting.en: Go to bed.

extensions.scene: You write it on a worksheet yourself, which is where it is entirely neutral — the same word doing an administrative job rather than a domestic one, and nobody reads anything into it.
extensions.jp: 質問に答えなさい。
extensions.en: Answer the question.

extensions.scene: Downward only. Used at a colleague it does not read as brisk, it reads as talking to them like a child, and adult-to-adult requests stay with the forms from Step 5.
extensions.jp: 答えてください。
extensions.en: Please answer — the sideways version.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
質問 is Step 22 bank; used one step early.

items.step: Step 20 · Doing to & being done to

setting.scene: One shape, three readings, all arriving in the same fortnight: it can be done, it was done to me, and the polite form of a verb. Nothing on the page separates them. The rest of the sentence has to do the disambiguating, which is why this collision gets a lesson of its own.
setting.jp: ここから山が見られます。
setting.en: The mountain can be seen from here — potential.

extensions.scene: You build the other reading of the identical shape, where something happened to somebody rather than being possible, and only the particles and the surrounding context tell the two of them apart.
extensions.jp: 先生に名前を聞かれました。
extensions.en: The teacher asked me my name — passive.

extensions.t: ら抜き — 見れる, 食べれる for the potential — is widespread, genuinely useful because it disambiguates, and still marked wrong in formal writing. Recognise both; write the long one.
extensions.scene: Half the people around you drop the ら in speech, which removes the ambiguity you have just spent a lesson learning to live with — and a marker will still take it off you in writing.
extensions.jp: 見れる
extensions.en: Spoken potential, ら dropped — clear, common, and marked wrong on paper.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
山 is outside the Step 20 bank; from the module's own example.

setting.scene: Somebody is choosing where to take a visiting inspector to lunch and has asked you, which means your answer needs to sound like a recommendation rather than a single reason. You have three reasons and no wish to rank them, and there is a joint that stacks them while implying there are more.
setting.jp: 安いし、おいしいし、あの店がいいですよ。
setting.en: It's cheap, it's good — that place is the one.

extensions.scene: You use it about why you are not going out on Sunday, where the same open-ended stacking works as a soft excuse — reasons among others, none of them the whole story.
extensions.jp: 雨だし、時間もないし。
extensions.en: It's raining, I've no time…

extensions.scene: One of these is enough to change the flavour. Even a single one hints at unnamed more, where the から from Step 11 names the reason and closes the list.
extensions.jp: 安いから、あの店がいいですよ。
extensions.en: から names THE reason; し leaves the list open.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You spent Saturday morning making something to take to a barbecue — the four-hour version, from scratch, because you wanted to turn up with something real. You arrive and there are three of the same thing already on the table, all shop-bought, and yours goes home again untouched.
setting.jp: 勉強したのに、忘れてしまいました。
setting.en: I studied — and still forgot.

extensions.scene: You say it about the barbecue itself rather than about studying, and the joint carries an ache that the neutral but from Step 11 simply does not have available to it.
extensions.jp: 作ったのに、誰も食べませんでした。
extensions.en: I made it, and nobody ate any.

extensions.scene: Left trailing and unfinished, it is reproach distilled — and the sentence does not need completing at all, because the ache inside it is already whole without any second half.
extensions.jp: せっかく作ったのに…
extensions.en: After I went to all that trouble…

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Sports day again, the forecast is bad, and somebody has to say out loud what happens if it rains — because the answer is that it goes ahead regardless. That is a concession rather than a condition: the rain is granted first, and then overridden.
setting.jp: 雨が降っても、行きます。
setting.en: Even if it rains, I'm going.

extensions.scene: You use it about a price rather than about the weather, conceding the objection and then continuing straight past it, which is exactly what makes this different from an if.
extensions.jp: 高くても、買います。
extensions.en: Even if it's pricey, I'm buying it.

extensions.scene: Same rain, opposite spines: one form cancels the plan and this one overrides it. And the permission question from Step 5 was this joint all along — even if I do this, is it all right?
extensions.jp: 降ったら行きません / 降っても行きます
extensions.en: たら cancels; ても overrides.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Telling a story of any length in Japanese means joining sentences rather than clauses, and the words that do that are not the ones you have been using inside sentences. Half of storytelling is the noises the listener makes, and one of these words is theirs rather than yours.
setting.jp: 雨が降りました。それで、家にいました。
setting.en: It rained. So I stayed in.

extensions.scene: You add the one that piles on rather than concludes, which is what you want when the second sentence is more of the same rather than a consequence of the first.
extensions.jp: 安いです。それに、おいしいです。
extensions.en: It's cheap. And what's more, it's good.

extensions.scene: Two social traps in one lesson. Opening a reply with the because-word can land as like-I-said; and the bare so-then with the pitch rising is the listener's nudge for you to keep going.
extensions.jp: それで？
extensions.en: …and then? — the listener's nudge, not yours.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Three ways to say but, and they are not interchangeable — they are three temperatures. One notes the contrast and moves on. One grants the objection and continues anyway. One aches. Picking the hot one for a trivial contrast is the error, and it reads as sulking.
setting.jp: 高いですが、買います。
setting.en: Pricey, but I'm buying it — cool.

extensions.scene: You build the middle temperature about the same purchase, conceding the price rather than merely noting it in passing, which is a different claim about how much the objection actually weighed.
extensions.jp: 高くても、買います。
extensions.en: Even if it's pricey, I'm buying it.

extensions.t: のに is the strong stuff. Spent on trivia it reads as sulking; saved for a real betrayal of expectation it lands perfectly. When unsure, けど is never wrong — it is the neutral setting and nobody has ever been offended by it.
extensions.scene: You use the hot one about a shop being shut on a Tuesday, which is not a betrayal of anything, and it comes out sounding like a complaint about the universe.
extensions.jp: 高いのに、買いました。
extensions.en: Save this heat for something that deserves it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The section head asks whether you are coming back next year and the honest answer is that you have not decided. Saying that in Japanese needs the undecided thing packed into a box and dropped into a sentence about deciding — a whole question, boxed, sitting where a noun would sit.
setting.jp: 行くかどうか、まだ決めていません。
setting.en: Whether I'll go — still undecided.

extensions.scene: You ask her something in the same shape about a meeting nobody has confirmed yet, and the box behaves like any other noun in the sentence once it has been closed up.
extensions.jp: 会議があるかどうか、わかりません。
extensions.en: I don't know whether there's a meeting.

extensions.scene: The politeness comes off inside the box. Boxes take plain contents only, and leaving the polite ending in is the error that marks a sentence as assembled rather than as spoken.
extensions.jp: 学生かどうか
extensions.en: Never 学生ですかどうか — plain inside the box.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Same machinery as the last lesson, open question this time. Not whether somebody is coming but who — and the who has to go inside the box along with the rest of the question, after which the whole box sits inside a sentence about not knowing.
setting.jp: 誰が来るか、わかりません。
setting.en: Who's coming — no idea.

extensions.scene: You build one about a word rather than a person, which is the shape half your questions will take for the next year — asking about the content of something you cannot yet read.
extensions.jp: どういう意味か、わかりません。
extensions.en: I don't know what it means.

extensions.scene: Collision with Step 11: the same two kana standing alone mean somebody. The verb inside the box is the tell — a boxed question has one, and an indefinite has nothing at all.
extensions.jp: 誰か / 誰が来るか
extensions.en: Somebody / who's coming — the verb tells you which.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Two sentences about your younger brother five minutes apart. In the first you are reporting something you heard through the wall at eleven last night. In the second you are telling somebody what he is like — a standing fact, true whether or not anybody is listening.
setting.jp: 弟が歌うのを聞きました。
setting.en: I heard my brother singing — live, sensed.

extensions.scene: The second sentence steps back out of the moment and into a standing fact about him, and the nominaliser cools accordingly — same brother, same verb, an entirely different distance.
extensions.jp: 弟は歌うことが好きです。
extensions.en: He likes singing.

extensions.scene: Where both fit, one runs warm and spoken and the other cool and written. Where the houses are fixed there is no choice at all, and there are only two of those.
extensions.jp: 読むのが好き / 読むことが好き
extensions.en: Warm and spoken / cool and written.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A word on a notice on the staffroom door that you can read aloud and cannot understand, which is a different problem from the one you have been solving all year. Up to now you have been asking what things are called. This asks what something means, and they are not the same question.
setting.jp: すみません、どういう意味ですか。
setting.en: Sorry — what does that mean?

extensions.scene: You use it about a word somebody says rather than one you read, and it is the single most useful sentence in this step — the one that keeps a conversation going instead of ending it.
extensions.jp: その言葉はどういう意味ですか。
extensions.en: What does that word mean?

extensions.scene: Keep the two learner-questions apart. One asks for the word and grows your vocabulary forwards; the other asks for the sense and grows it backwards from something you already met.
extensions.jp: 何といいますか / どういう意味ですか
extensions.en: What's it called / what does it mean.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Two nominalisers, and most of the time either one will do — which is exactly why the few places that refuse one of them are worth memorising rather than reasoning about. There are two fixed houses in the language and everything outside them is taste.
setting.jp: 泳ぐことができます。
setting.en: I can swim — a fixed house, こと.

extensions.scene: You build the other fixed house, the experience one from Step 18, and it takes the same nominaliser for the same reason — the construction owns it, and no judgement is involved.
extensions.jp: 行ったことがあります。
extensions.en: I've been — the other fixed house.

extensions.t: The error that grates most is の in こと's fixed house — 話すのができます. The fixed houses are few: 〜ことができる and 〜たことがある, always こと. Guard those two and the rest of the choice is taste rather than grammar.
extensions.scene: You put the warm spoken one into the ability construction, which is the one place in the language it cannot go, and the sentence stops being Japanese at that exact syllable.
extensions.jp: 話すのができます
extensions.en: Wrong — ことができる owns its noun.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
泳ぐ is outside the Step 22 bank; from the module's own example.

setting.scene: A boy in your class has been at the window for ten minutes while the rest are outside. He has not said anything and you have not asked. You mention it to the teacher next to you, and what you have is what you can see — not what he told you, and not what you know.
setting.jp: 弟は公園へ行きたがっています。
setting.en: My brother's desperate to go to the park.

extensions.scene: You say your own version of the same want straight out, because your own head is the one place you are allowed to report from directly — and the contrast between the two sentences is the whole lesson.
extensions.jp: 私は行きたいです。
extensions.en: I want to go.

extensions.scene: The particle moves along with the machinery. Your own want leans on one of them; the observed behaviour takes the other, because a state has become something you are watching somebody do.
extensions.jp: 水が飲みたい / 水を飲みたがっている
extensions.en: State takes が; observed behaviour takes を.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Your sister has walked past the same shop window four times this month and has mentioned the bag in it twice without ever saying she wants it. You are not claiming to know her mind — you are reporting what anybody watching would have noticed, which is a different sentence.
setting.jp: 妹は新しいかばんをほしがっています。
setting.en: My sister's got her eye on a new bag.

extensions.scene: Your own version of the same want takes the plain form and the other particle, and putting the two sentences side by side is the fastest way to feel the line the language is drawing.
extensions.jp: 私はかばんがほしいです。
extensions.en: I want a bag.

extensions.scene: The particle swap is not decoration, it is the grammar itself: one marks the target of a state, the other marks the object of behaviour that you are standing there watching.
extensions.jp: かばんがほしい / かばんをほしがっている
extensions.en: State keeps が; behaviour takes を.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: One line runs through the whole language and this is where it gets named: inner states are first-person territory. Your own wants go flat. Everyone else's reach you as signs, as appearances, or as words they said — and claiming direct access to another mind is the error this drill hunts.
setting.jp: 私は行きたいです。
setting.en: Mine — stated directly.

extensions.scene: You report somebody else's want three different ways in one conversation — what you can see, what it looks like, and what they actually told you — and none of the three claims to be inside their head.
extensions.jp: 行きたいと言っています。
extensions.en: He says he wants to go — reported, not claimed.

extensions.t: Questions are the exception that proves the rule: 行きたいですか asks the person directly, so たい is fine there — you are requesting the first-person report rather than faking it. The restriction is on asserting somebody else's insides, not on discussing them.
extensions.scene: You ask a colleague what she wants to do at the weekend using the plain form, and it is entirely correct — because asking somebody is not the same as claiming to know.
extensions.jp: 何がしたいですか。
extensions.en: What do you want to do? — asking is fine.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody at work tells you the section head is coming, and uses a word you have never heard for it. You have been in this country long enough to order food, register an address and argue with a phone company, and a single sentence about somebody walking down a corridor has just gone past you completely. This is the point where most learners decide keigo is a wall.
setting.jp: 日本語を話します。
setting.en: I speak Japanese — 丁寧語, and it is already keigo.

extensions.scene: It is not a wall, and the proof is the sentence you have been saying since your first week. です・ます is 丁寧語. 丁寧語 is 敬語. You have been standing under this umbrella for twenty-three steps without anybody telling you what it was called.
extensions.jp: 田中と申します。
extensions.en: My name is Tanaka — the same umbrella, one direction further.

extensions.scene: Step 5 taught you お茶 and ご飯 and called them polish. They had a name. And the interesting half is the ones that escaped — nobody hears politeness in ご飯 any more, because it stopped being a choice and became the word.
extensions.jp: ご飯・お名前・おビール
extensions.en: Frozen / a live dial / marked — one prefix, three jobs.

extensions.scene: One honest footnote, because the tidy four-room map you have just been handed is a simplification, and the fuller official version has five rooms rather than four. You will meet the extra one eventually and it is better not to be surprised by it.
extensions.jp: 尊敬語・謙譲語Ⅰ・謙譲語Ⅱ・丁寧語・美化語
extensions.en: The official five, 2007 — this app teaches four.

claims: The Agency for Cultural Affairs' 敬語の指針 (2 February 2007) classifies keigo into five categories: 尊敬語, 謙譲語Ⅰ, 謙譲語Ⅱ (丁重語), 丁寧語, 美化語
です・ます is 丁寧語 and is therefore a category of 敬語
美化語 splits in practice into frozen (ご飯, お腹, お菓子), optional (お水, お名前) and marked (おビール) uses
お attaches to 和語, ご to 漢語, and loanwords take neither
flags: A search result mis-dated 敬語の指針 to 2019. It is 平成19年 = 2007. Recorded so it cannot propagate.
The three-tier 美化語 split is a practical description rather than an official category; the reviewer should confirm the frozen examples.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You ring the school office to ask whether a particular teacher is in today, and you have the sentence ready — you have had it since Step 8. 先生はいますか. What comes back is not an answer to that question but a version of it you did not recognise, asked back at you for confirmation.
setting.jp: 先生はいますか。
setting.en: Is the teacher in? — the sentence you own.

extensions.scene: What the office says is the same question with the teacher lifted a floor. Nothing about the grammar around it changed — only the verb, and only because of whose being-there it describes.
extensions.jp: 先生は今日、学校にいらっしゃいますか。
extensions.en: Is the teacher at school today? — their action, raised.

extensions.scene: These verbs conjugate politely in a shape that will trip your ear before it trips your grammar, because they put an い where everything you know about る-verbs expects a り.
extensions.jp: いらっしゃいます・おっしゃいます・なさいます
extensions.en: Not いらっしゃります — the -aru verbs go irregular here.

extensions.scene: And nothing in this lesson is for your own sentences yet. Elevated verbs describe the other person, so pointed at yourself they do the one thing the whole system cannot say — which is why this step asks you only to recognise them.
extensions.jp: 私はいらっしゃいます。
extensions.en: Wrong — you cannot elevate yourself.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Three verbs you have kept carefully apart since Step 4 — being somewhere, going, coming — are about to become one word, and then a different one word depending on which way the sentence points. This is the single hardest recognition problem in the stage and it is worth slowing down for, because you will meet it on a platform this evening.
setting.jp: 先生はいますか。行きますか。来ますか。
setting.en: Three separate questions — for now.

extensions.scene: Going up, all three collapse into one. Which means the sentence you hear back is genuinely three questions wearing one coat, and the room rather than the grammar tells you which was meant.
extensions.jp: 先生はいらっしゃいますか。
extensions.en: Is the teacher in — or coming? Both, and context decides.

extensions.scene: Coming down, two of them collapse into a different word — and you will hear it first not from a person but from a loudspeaker, several times a day, for as long as you live here.
extensions.jp: まもなく電車が参ります。
extensions.en: The train will arrive shortly — the company lowering its own train.

extensions.scene: The expensive mistake is aiming a down-verb at the person you meant to raise, and it is an easy one to make, because both words mean the same plain thing underneath and only the direction separates them.
extensions.jp: 先生はおりますか。
extensions.en: Wrong — おる sends the teacher down.

claims: 参ります in station announcements is the humble form used by the operator about its own train
いらっしゃる serves as the honorific replacement for いる, 行く and 来る
参る serves as the humble replacement for 行く and 来る; 伺う is narrower (visiting, asking)
flags: Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: A hotel lobby, and you ask where the toilets are. You know exactly how this sentence works — お手洗いはどこにありますか — because あります has been yours since Step 8. The answer comes back with the shape intact and the verb replaced by something that sounds like it belongs to the building rather than to the person saying it.
setting.jp: お手洗いはどこにありますか。
setting.en: Where is the restroom? — the sentence you own.

extensions.scene: What you get is あります in formal dress. It honours nobody in particular — it is politeness aimed at the room at large, which is exactly why buildings speak it and friends never do.
extensions.jp: お手洗いは二階にございます。
extensions.en: The restroom is on the second floor.

extensions.scene: The negative is the shop's gentle no, and it is worth recognising before you need it — it is how a full restaurant turns you away without ever saying the word.
extensions.jp: 申し訳ありません、席がございません。
extensions.en: Our apologies — there are no seats.

extensions.scene: And you have been saying one of these every day for a year without noticing it. The thanks you give a cashier, a driver and a colleague has ござる sitting quietly inside it, doing exactly this job.
extensions.jp: ありがとうございます。
extensions.en: The ござる was there all along.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: A first meeting at a company, and the introduction is the one sentence you have rehearsed. 私は田中です. It is correct, it is polite, and it is not what anybody in the room is about to say about themselves — because introducing yourself is the doorway into the half of the system that points down.
setting.jp: 私は田中です。
setting.en: I'm Tanaka — correct, and not what gets said here.

extensions.scene: The version that gets said lowers your own act of naming yourself. It is the first humble verb almost every learner produces on purpose, and after it the rest of the set stops feeling exotic.
extensions.jp: 田中と申します。
extensions.en: My name is Tanaka — 言う, lowered.

extensions.scene: Every plain verb that has an up-form turns out to have a down-twin as well, and the two halves of the map finally sit beside each other rather than arriving a step apart.
extensions.jp: いる → いらっしゃる↑・おる↓
extensions.en: Up for them, down for you — one plain verb, two directions.

extensions.scene: And the verb you say before every meal takes its seat on that map. It has been sitting in the humble column since your very first week here, doing this exact job.
extensions.jp: いただきます。
extensions.en: もらう, lowered — and your eating and drinking with it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You answer the office phone. It is a customer asking for your section head — the man you would never mention without さん inside these walls, who signs your leave and sits four desks away. He is out until three. You have to say so, to somebody outside the company, and every instinct you own is about to give you the wrong sentence.
setting.jp: 田中さんは出かけています。
setting.en: Mr Tanaka is out — correct inside the office.

extensions.scene: Across the wall he loses his さん and takes a humble verb, and the thing to understand is that this is not disrespect aimed at him. You are lowering your entire side as one body, and the unity is the respect.
extensions.jp: 田中はただいま外出しております。
extensions.en: Tanaka is out at the moment.

extensions.t: The axis is not you-versus-them, it is your side versus outside — うち and そと. Step 3's cc-family planted the instinct long before you could use it: your own mother is 母 to outsiders and お母さん at home, which is the same rule running on a noun instead of a verb.
extensions.scene: The rule is older than this lesson. You have been switching between two words for your own mother since Step 3, on exactly this axis, without anybody calling it one.
extensions.jp: 母 / お母さん
extensions.en: Outward / at home — the same wall, drawn round a family.

extensions.t: And the axis MOVES. The same man is うち at work and そと at his daughter's school gate; the same colleague is うち to a customer and そと to your own section head. It is not a property of the person, it is a property of the boundary you are speaking across at that moment.
extensions.scene: At the school gate on Saturday you meet him again, in a room where you are both parents and neither of you is the company, and the whole thing rearranges itself.
extensions.jp: 田中さんもいらっしゃいますか。
extensions.en: Is Tanaka coming too? — outside work, he is そと and goes back up.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You need to say that the president has already gone home, and there is no special verb for it — the elevated list covers being, going, saying, eating, doing and looking, and 帰る is not on it. This is the moment the learner discovers the list is short and the language is not, and that keigo has a productive engine underneath the vocabulary.
setting.jp: 社長はもう帰りました。
setting.en: The president has already gone home — plain polite.

extensions.scene: Two patterns cover every verb the special list skips. お plus the stem plus になる raises theirs; お plus the stem plus する lowers yours. You have been hearing both since Step 26 without being told the formula.
extensions.jp: 社長はもうお帰りになりました。
extensions.en: The president has already gone home — raised.

extensions.scene: Where a special verb already exists it wins, and reaching for the pattern instead of the word sounds like somebody assembling their politeness out of a kit rather than speaking it.
extensions.jp: お食べになる
extensions.en: Off — 食べる already has 召し上がる.

extensions.scene: And the overreach that marks a nervous speaker more clearly than anything else is dressing the same verb twice over, when one dressing was the entire requirement and the second one only draws attention to the effort.
extensions.jp: ご覧になられる
extensions.en: 二重敬語 — one dressing per verb.

setting.scene: The same question — will you have coffee? — asked three times in one day. To a friend at lunch. To the colleague across the desk. To a visitor your section head has brought in, in the first thirty seconds of a meeting that matters. Three rooms, one question, and the whole system reduces to picking a height and holding it.
setting.jp: コーヒーを飲む？
setting.en: Want coffee? — plain, to a friend.

extensions.scene: The middle altitude is the one you have lived in since Step 1 and it is correct almost everywhere. The top one raises their verb — and note that only their verb moves, because the rest of the sentence has no altitude to have.
extensions.jp: コーヒーを召し上がりますか。
extensions.en: Will you have coffee? — their verb, raised.

extensions.t: Pick the altitude once and hold it. The error that gets noticed is not choosing the wrong level — it is drifting between them mid-conversation, which reads as unstable rather than casual. And never both directions on one verb: keigo is a costume for their verbs and a bow for your own.
extensions.scene: Halfway through the meeting you relax and a single plain form slips in among the elevated ones. Nobody says anything about it and nobody needs to, because everybody in the room heard it happen.
extensions.jp: いただきます。
extensions.en: Your own drinking, lowered — the other direction, on your verb.

extensions.t: And never keigo at a friend, where it lands as comedy or, worse, as distance. Using the top altitude on somebody close is not extra respect; it is a wall, and they will hear it as one.
extensions.scene: You try the elevated version on the friend you eat lunch with every day, as a joke, and it is funny for about one second and then quietly cold in a way neither of you wants.
extensions.jp: 召し上がりますか。
extensions.en: To a friend: comedy, then distance.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: The visa renewal came back approved, and it came back approved because somebody in the office spent forty minutes checking your paperwork line by line before you submitted it. Telling people it went through is easy. Telling them in a way that puts the credit where it belongs needs a word that から does not have.
setting.jp: 先生のおかげで、合格しました。
setting.en: Thanks to my teacher, I passed.

extensions.scene: You write the thank-you the same evening, and the word does the work your English would have needed a whole extra sentence for — it names the cause and hands over the credit in one move.
extensions.jp: 手伝ってくれたおかげで、間に合いました。
extensions.en: Thanks to your help, I made it in time.

extensions.t: It can be used sarcastically, and it lands hard when it is. 君のおかげで about a disaster is not a mistake anybody makes twice — the word is so firmly on the good side that putting a bad outcome behind it reads as a deliberate cut.
extensions.scene: Somebody uses it about a meeting that overran by two hours, and for a moment nobody in the room is quite sure whether it was a joke — which is how you learn that the word has only one side and putting a bad outcome behind it is always heard.
extensions.jp: 君のおかげで、二時間かかりました。
extensions.en: Thanks to you, that took two hours — and everybody heard the edge.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: The form came back rejected over a date written in the wrong order, and the twenty minutes you now have to spend fixing it are not really yours to be annoyed about — you filled it in. Explaining what happened needs a word that says where the fault sits, and Japanese will not let you leave that unsaid.
setting.jp: 寝坊したせいで、遅刻しました。
setting.en: I was late because I overslept.

extensions.scene: You use it about yourself first, which is where it is safest and where it reads as ordinary rather than accusatory — the blame lands on you and nobody has to react to it.
extensions.jp: 書き間違えたせいで、やり直しになりました。
extensions.en: Because I wrote it wrong, it has to be done again.

extensions.t: Aimed at a person it stops being a turn of phrase and becomes a real accusation. About yourself it is modest; about a colleague it is something you would have to mean, and there is a softer version — せいか — that turns the blame into a maybe.
extensions.scene: You nearly use it about the person who handed you the form in the first place, and stop, because the sentence would have been heard exactly as it was built — as blame, aimed at somebody standing two desks away.
extensions.jp: 疲れているせいか、間違えました。
extensions.en: Perhaps because I'm tired, I made a mistake — せいか hedges the blame.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: One box on the residence application, left blank because you were not sure whether it applied to you, and the whole thing has come back. Not the difficult parts — those were fine. One box. The sentence for this is not the same as the sentence for an ordinary mistake, because the size of the cause and the size of the result do not match.
setting.jp: 一言言わなかったばかりに、大きな問題になりました。
setting.en: Just because I didn't say one word, it turned into a real problem.

extensions.scene: You use it about something smaller and older — a message you did not send, and the fortnight of confusion that followed — and the pattern carries the regret without you having to add a word of it.
extensions.jp: 連絡しなかったばかりに、ずっと待たせてしまいました。
extensions.en: Just because I didn't get in touch, I kept them waiting all that time.

extensions.t: The disproportion is the entire point. A large cause with a large result is せいで's job — spend ばかりに on it and the pattern is wasted, because it promises unfairness and the sentence has not delivered any.
extensions.scene: You try it on something where the cause was genuinely serious and the result proportionate, and it comes out sounding like an excuse rather than a regret, because the pattern promises unfairness the facts do not supply.
extensions.jp: 準備しなかったせいで、失敗しました。
extensions.en: A real cause, a real result — that is せいで, not ばかりに.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Four ways to say because, and you now have all of them. The difference between them is not politeness and it is not formality — it is whether the reason has an owner, and if so, whether that owner comes out of the sentence looking good or bad.
setting.jp: 雨だから、行きません。
setting.en: It's raining, so I'm not going — から asserts, and owns nothing.

extensions.scene: You rewrite the same explanation three times to watch the dial move, and only the middle word changes each time — neutral, then credited, then blamed. The facts are identical in all three sentences and the reader's impression is not.
extensions.jp: 晴れたおかげで、できました。
extensions.en: It cleared up, so we managed it — and the weather gets the credit.

extensions.t: The error here is social rather than grammatical, which makes it the expensive kind. 雨のおかげで試合が中止になりました thanks the rain for ruining the match: perfectly formed, and it reads as sarcasm whether or not any was intended.
extensions.scene: So you check each sentence against its outcome before sending it, which takes about a second and turns out to be the whole discipline of this step — good result with the credit word, bad result with the blame word, and never crossed.
extensions.jp: 雨のせいで、中止になりました。
extensions.en: Bad outcome, blaming word — matched.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Your first real email in Japanese that is not a request — a short note to the section about a change to the timetable. You know how to say the timetable and you know how to say changed, and you do not know how to say the sentence is ABOUT the timetable, which turns out to be the thing the whole email hangs on.
setting.jp: この問題について話しましょう。
setting.en: Let's talk about this problem.

extensions.scene: You use it in the subject line as well, where it becomes についての and sits in front of a noun — which is how every notice on the staffroom wall has always been written.
extensions.jp: 時間割についてのお知らせ
extensions.en: A notice regarding the timetable.

extensions.t: It needs a verb that can take a subject matter. 問題について行きます is not a sentence — you cannot go about a problem — and the mistake is easy because English lets about attach to almost anything.
extensions.scene: You write a sentence where について sits in front of a verb of movement, and it comes apart in a way nothing in English would have warned you about, because English lets about attach to nearly anything and Japanese does not.
extensions.jp: 問題について考えました。
extensions.en: I thought about the problem — a verb that can hold a topic.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A parent has written in with a complaint, and you have been asked to draft the reply. The complaint is the thing you are answering — not the thing you are discussing — and Japanese keeps those two apart with two different particles that English blurs into one word.
setting.jp: 質問に対して、はっきり答えました。
setting.en: I answered the question clearly.

extensions.scene: You use it again in the same reply, about the school's position on the issue, where it points a stance at a target rather than naming a subject — and the noun in front is something being faced rather than discussed.
extensions.jp: その問題に対する学校の考えを説明しました。
extensions.en: I explained the school's position on the matter.

extensions.t: The overlap with について is real and the test is one question: can the noun be a topic of conversation, or is it something you are facing? You think ABOUT a problem and answer TO a question, and the two particles split exactly there.
extensions.scene: You swap the two particles once by accident and the sentence says you discussed the question rather than answered it, which is a different and noticeably more evasive claim to be making in a letter to a parent.
extensions.jp: 質問について話しました。
extensions.en: I discussed the question — which is not the same as answering it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A form asking how you would like to be contacted, with a note underneath explaining that the answer varies depending on which office you are dealing with. Three separate uses of one particle on a single sheet of paper, and none of them is the one you learned first.
setting.jp: 人によって、意見が違います。
setting.en: Opinions differ from person to person.

extensions.scene: You meet the second use the same afternoon, in a sentence about how a decision was reached rather than about how much things vary — the means rather than the variation, and nothing in the shape of the word tells you which.
extensions.jp: この方法によって、問題が解決しました。
extensions.en: The problem was solved by this method.

extensions.t: The third use is the passive agent, and it is the written one. In speech the agent takes に; によって belongs to reports and documents, so swapping them makes writing sound spoken and speech sound like a memo.
extensions.scene: You see it again on a notice about a building and realise it is doing the job に does in conversation, which is why formal Japanese reads as though it were written by a different language from the one spoken in the corridor.
extensions.jp: この本は夏目漱石によって書かれました。
extensions.en: This book was written by Sōseki — the written passive agent.

claims: によって serves as the agent marker in formal written passives, where speech uses に
flags: 夏目漱石 uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: The letter confirming your contract renewal, which is one page long and contains no sentence you would ever say out loud. Halfway down is a word doing the job で does, in clothes で never wears, and recognising it is the difference between reading the letter and guessing at it.
setting.jp: 会議において、その問題が話し合われました。
setting.en: The matter was discussed at the meeting.

extensions.scene: You meet it again the same week on a notice about environmental policy, where it marks a field rather than a place — and the register is identical both times, which is the only thing the word reliably signals.
extensions.jp: 日本における環境の問題
extensions.en: Environmental issues in Japan.

extensions.t: It does not stretch to ordinary places. 台所において料理します is wrong in the way a dinner jacket is wrong at breakfast: で is the word, and において is reserved for the abstract, the institutional and the ceremonial.
extensions.scene: You try it about your own kitchen as an experiment and it is immediately, obviously absurd — the word simply will not sit on a small physical place, and で snaps back into position without any effort at all.
extensions.jp: 台所で料理します。
extensions.en: In the kitchen — で, and nothing else.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A reference letter you have been asked to write for a colleague who is moving on, and the sentence that matters is the one about what the work meant to her. Not what it was — what it was to her, which is a different claim and needs a word that marks whose view it is.
setting.jp: 私にとって、この経験はとても大切です。
setting.en: For me, this experience matters a great deal.

extensions.scene: You use it about yourself in a form asking why you want to take the course, and it turns a flat statement into a positioned one — the same fact, now clearly a judgement made from somewhere rather than a claim about the world.
extensions.jp: 私にとって、日本語は仕事の一部です。
extensions.en: For me, Japanese is part of the job.

extensions.t: The trap is plain に. 私に大切です is not the sentence — it is 私にとって大切です. And what follows must be a judgement rather than an action: にとって働きます is not a thing, because working is not an evaluation.
extensions.scene: You write it once with に alone and the sentence is not quite ungrammatical, only wrong in a way you cannot yet hear — which is the most expensive kind of error, because nothing in the room corrects it.
extensions.jp: 学生にとって、その本は少し難しいです。
extensions.en: For students, that book is a little difficult.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Five shapes that all start with に, all take a noun, and all get translated as about or for at some point — which is exactly why meeting them one at a time is the slowest possible way to learn them. Laid out together they stop overlapping.
setting.jp: 問題について話す
setting.en: Discuss the problem — subject matter.

extensions.scene: You sort your own last three emails by which of the five each sentence actually needed, and two of them turn out to have been wrong in a way nobody mentioned at the time and nobody was ever going to.
extensions.jp: 質問に対して答える
extensions.en: Answer the question — facing it, not discussing it.

extensions.t: When none of the five feels right, the plain particle usually was right all along. These are for when a sentence needs the extra distance — a noun held out as subject matter — and a paragraph that uses three of them reads as somebody testing new vocabulary.
extensions.scene: You take two of them back out of a draft and it reads better immediately — which is the lesson underneath the lesson, because these are for distance and a paragraph does not need distance in every sentence.
extensions.jp: 私にとって大切です。
extensions.en: Important to me — the viewpoint one, and the one worth keeping.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Somebody in the staffroom mentions, in passing, that you have been here eleven years. The person they are telling had assumed two or three, and you watch the arithmetic happen on their face. What they say next is not a question and not a new fact — it is the sound of something clicking into place.
setting.jp: 十年住んでいるんですか。道理で日本語が上手なわけですね。
setting.en: Ten years? No wonder your Japanese is good.

extensions.scene: You use it yourself an hour later, when somebody explains why the trains were a mess all morning, and the whole of your journey suddenly makes sense backwards rather than forwards.
extensions.jp: 事故があったんですか。だから遅れたわけですね。
extensions.en: There was an accident? So that's why everyone was late.

extensions.t: It cannot open a conversation. わけだ concludes from something already on the table, so used cold it sounds like the end of a thought nobody heard the beginning of. And it is not から — から supplies a reason, わけだ receives one.
extensions.scene: You try it as an opening line and the other person waits for the part that was supposed to come first, because the word is a receipt for information rather than a delivery of it.
extensions.jp: 電車が止まっていたから、遅れました。
extensions.en: から supplies the reason. わけだ would have received it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: You have said, honestly, that you do not eat much natto — and you can see the conclusion forming on the other side of the table, which is that you hate it. You do not hate it. Denying that flatly would deny the thing you actually said, so what you need is a way to deny the inference and keep the fact.
setting.jp: 嫌いなわけではありませんが、あまり食べません。
setting.en: It's not that I dislike it — I just don't eat much of it.

extensions.scene: You use it about your own Japanese the same week, when somebody's compliment has drawn a conclusion considerably larger than the evidence supports and denying it flatly would be its own kind of dishonesty.
extensions.jp: 全部わかったわけではありません。
extensions.en: It's not that I understood all of it.

extensions.t: It denies the inference, not the sentence. 全部わかったわけではありません means I did not understand ALL of it — not that I understood none. The difference matters, because the second is a far bigger claim and English speakers reach for it by accident.
extensions.scene: You hear the same shape used to walk back an impression without retracting a single word of fact, which is most of what it is for and most of why adults reach for it constantly.
extensions.jp: 行きたくないわけじゃないです。
extensions.en: It's not that I don't want to go — the door stays open.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A colleague has been covering for somebody who has not asked and has not thanked her, and she has not said anything about it for three weeks. You are about to give an opinion that is not advice and not a rule — it is a judgement about what a person ought to do, and Japanese has a word that carries exactly that weight.
setting.jp: もっと早く言うべきでした。
setting.en: You should have said something sooner.

extensions.scene: You use the negative version about yourself, about something you said in a meeting and regretted before the sentence had finished leaving your mouth — which is where this pattern is safest and most honest.
extensions.jp: そんなことを言うべきではありませんでした。
extensions.en: I shouldn't have said that.

extensions.t: It is heavier than English should. 帰るべきです to a colleague is not go home and rest — it is closer to you ought to leave, and it will be heard as a judgement rather than a kindness. For gentle advice, Step 16's たらどうですか is the tool.
extensions.scene: You nearly use it to suggest that somebody take a break, and swap it for the softer pattern in time, because what you meant was kindness and what the word carries is a verdict.
extensions.jp: 少し休んだらどうですか。
extensions.en: How about a rest? — advice, not judgement.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: The office is dark, the section head's coat is gone from the hook, and the meeting she called for four o'clock is nine minutes from starting. You did not see her leave. Everything you have is evidence, and the sentence you want is the strongest thing you can say that is still, honestly, a guess.
setting.jp: 電気が消えている。もう帰ったに違いない。
setting.en: The lights are off — she must have gone home.

extensions.scene: You use it about an object rather than a person, on handwriting you recognise without having watched anybody write it — the evidence is complete and the conclusion still is not a fact.
extensions.jp: この字は先生のに違いありません。
extensions.en: This handwriting must be the teacher's.

extensions.t: It is a conclusion, not a fact. Used about something you actually witnessed it sounds like you are guessing about your own experience — and it is noticeably more written than spoken, where きっと does the same job with less weight.
extensions.scene: Somebody says it out loud in conversation and it sounds a shade formal, which is how you learn where it actually lives — in writing and in reasoning, rather than in the staffroom.
extensions.jp: きっと帰りましたよ。
extensions.en: She'll have gone home — the spoken version.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A first-year teacher has made the same mistake you made in your first year, and is taking it considerably harder than it deserves. What you want to say is not about this mistake — it is about how the world generally goes, which is a different kind of claim and needs a different ending.
setting.jp: 若い時は、失敗するものです。
setting.en: When you're young, you make mistakes — that's how it goes.

extensions.scene: The same word turns up that evening doing something quite different, when somebody older begins a sentence about how things used to be — the nostalgia use, which is far more common in speech than the general truth.
extensions.jp: 学生の頃は、よく遊んだものです。
extensions.en: Back in our student days, we used to go out a lot.

extensions.t: It cannot describe one situation. 今日は寒いものです is wrong, because today's weather is not a general truth — the claim has to be one that would still hold next year. That restriction is what separates it from です.
extensions.scene: You try it about a single cold afternoon and it lands as though you were legislating about the weather, because the pattern claims a truth that would still hold next year.
extensions.jp: 今日は寒いです。
extensions.en: Today is cold — a fact about today, so plain です.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Six ways to say how sure you are, built across three stages, and this is the first time they sit on one line. The gap between neighbouring stops is not decorative — each one commits you to a different amount, and English collapses the middle four into might and probably.
setting.jp: 明日は雨でしょう。
setting.en: Probably rain — the forecast's own word.

extensions.scene: You place your own claims on the dial for a day and find you have been living at two stops out of six, which is why so much of what you say comes out either vaguer or firmer than you meant.
extensions.jp: 買ったから、来るはずです。
extensions.en: He bought a ticket, so he should be coming.

extensions.t: わけだ sits outside this line entirely. It is not a degree of certainty — it is a conclusion drawn from one, which is why it needs something already said before it can work at all.
extensions.scene: You notice the difference the moment you try to open a sentence with わけだ and cannot — it needs something already on the table, which none of the six stops on the dial do.
extensions.jp: 電気が消えている。帰ったに違いない。
extensions.en: Must have — the top of the dial, and the evidence closes it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A reading habit you have been meaning to build for two years finally starts on a Tuesday, with a book you will take four months to finish. Reporting that it has begun needs a shape that bolts one verb onto another — and it is the easiest member of a family you will use constantly.
setting.jp: 八時に読みはじめました。
setting.en: I started reading at eight.

extensions.scene: You use it about the weather within the hour, and notice that the compound works perfectly well on things nobody chose to start, which is not obvious from a pattern that looks like it is about intention.
extensions.jp: 雨が降りはじめました。
extensions.en: It's started raining.

extensions.t: はじめる is the transitive twin and はじまる the intransitive one, but the compound only ever takes はじめる — 雨が降りはじまる is wrong even though the rain starts by itself. The compound describes the action, not the rain's autonomy.
extensions.scene: You reach for the wrong twin and the sentence is rejected by a rule that has nothing to do with who did the starting — the compound describes the action, and the action always takes はじめる.
extensions.jp: 雨が降りはじめました。
extensions.en: The rain starts itself, and the compound still takes はじめる.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Four months later, the last page. The book has been on the desk long enough that finishing it is genuinely an event, and the sentence for it closes an action that had a length — which is what separates this from the ending you learned in Step 13.
setting.jp: この本を読みおわりました。
setting.en: I've finished reading this book.

extensions.scene: You use it about something smaller in order to arrange the evening, where the finishing is a condition for the next thing to happen rather than an announcement worth making in its own right.
extensions.jp: 食べおわったら、行きましょう。
extensions.en: Let's go once we've finished eating.

extensions.t: It does not work on verbs with no duration. 死におわる is not a sentence — a thing has to take time before it can finish — and instantaneous verbs take Step 13's てしまう instead, which finishes an action and adds a feeling.
extensions.scene: You test it on something momentary and the compound simply refuses to attach, because a thing has to take some amount of time before it can be finished, and forgetting takes none at all.
extensions.jp: 忘れてしまいました。
extensions.en: Forgetting has no duration, so it takes てしまう.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Your desk, honestly described: three books with markers in them, a form filled in as far as the third box, and a message to the landlord that has been sitting half-typed since Thursday. English needs a whole phrase for each of those. Japanese puts it inside the verb.
setting.jp: 読みかけの本が三冊あります。
setting.en: I've got three books on the go.

extensions.scene: You use it about a sentence rather than an object — the thing you started to say in the meeting and then decided against — which is the same unfinishedness applied to speech.
extensions.jp: 何か言いかけて、やめました。
extensions.en: He started to say something, then stopped.

extensions.t: It is not 〜ている. 食べています is eating, in progress, with somebody at the table. 食べかけています is left half-eaten and the room is empty. One is an action; the other is the state something got abandoned in.
extensions.scene: You use the wrong one about a plate on the table and describe somebody eating who in fact left an hour ago, which is a small error with a surprisingly large gap inside it.
extensions.jp: 食べかけのケーキがあります。
extensions.en: There's a half-eaten cake — a state, not an action.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
