setting.scene: The application you have been assembling for five weeks, with the certified translations and the two documents that had to come from another country, finally goes in. Saying you completed it is true and thin. There is a verb ending that says you completed it and that completing it cost something.
setting.jp: 最後まで走りぬきました。
setting.en: I ran it all the way to the end.

extensions.scene: You use it about the thinking rather than the doing, which is where it is most at home — a decision made properly rather than quickly, and the effort is inside the verb rather than beside it.
extensions.jp: よく考えぬいて決めました。
extensions.en: I thought it through properly before deciding.

extensions.t: Do not spend it on easy things. 食べぬきました about a sandwich is comic, because the pattern promises difficulty and an easy object undercuts it — for ordinary completion the words are おわる or てしまう.
extensions.scene: Somebody uses it about a completely trivial task as a joke, and the joke works precisely because the ending is far too heavy for the thing it has been asked to carry.
extensions.jp: 読みおわりました。
extensions.en: Ordinary completion — おわる, with no struggle claimed.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: The staffroom heater has been running since Friday, the window beside it has been open the same length of time, and it is Monday morning. Somebody is going to say something about it, and the word they use will contain the complaint so their voice does not have to.
setting.jp: 電気がつけっぱなしでした。
setting.en: The light had been left on.

extensions.scene: You use it as a request rather than a complaint, which is the polite half of the same word and the version you will actually produce more often than the accusing one.
extensions.jp: 窓を開けっぱなしにしないでください。
extensions.en: Please don't leave the window open.

extensions.t: It carries blame, so it is not the neutral way to report a state. Step 13's てある says somebody did it on purpose — 窓が開けてある — while っぱなし says somebody left it and should not have. Same window, two different accusations.
extensions.scene: You use てある where you meant っぱなし and accidentally credit somebody with having opened the window on purpose, which turns a complaint into a compliment that nobody in the room had earned.
extensions.jp: 窓が開けてあります。
extensions.en: Opened on purpose — the neutral report, with no blame in it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Five endings that all bolt onto a ます-stem and all change what the verb claims about its own completeness. Met one at a time they look like vocabulary; laid out together they are a system with two axes — how far the action got, and how you feel about that.
setting.jp: 読みかけの本
setting.en: Half-read — かける.

extensions.scene: You run a single verb through all five endings in a notebook and the two axes separate cleanly for the first time: began, finished, abandoned, endured, neglected — one stem, five different claims about completeness.
extensions.jp: 最後までやりぬいた。
extensions.en: Saw it through — ぬく, and it was hard.

extensions.t: The two worth drilling are the two with no English equivalent — かける and ぬく. English speakers reach for them last because nothing in a first language suggests that a verb could carry unfinishedness or endurance as part of its own shape.
extensions.scene: You catch yourself describing a half-done thing in three English-shaped words and then in one Japanese one, which is the first time the compound verbs feel like an economy rather than a burden.
extensions.jp: つけっぱなし
extensions.en: Left on — and it shouldn't have been.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A health check questionnaire with a column that is not asking whether you have been ill but whether you tend to be. One is an event and the other is a pattern, and the form wants the pattern — which needs a word that grades a tendency rather than reporting an occasion.
setting.jp: 最近、忘れがちです。
setting.en: I've been forgetful lately.

extensions.scene: You use it about your own childhood in the next box down, where a tendency across years rather than a fact about one week is exactly what the form is asking for.
extensions.jp: 子どもの頃は病気がちでした。
extensions.en: I was often ill as a child.

extensions.t: The negative colouring is built in. 元気がち is not a sentence, because being well a lot is not a complaint — if the tendency is welcome, this is not the word, and no amount of context will make it fit.
extensions.scene: You try it on something good and the sentence quietly refuses to mean anything, because the negative colouring is not connotation you can override with context — it is what the word is.
extensions.jp: よく元気になります。
extensions.en: Often gets better — plain, because がち cannot carry good news.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Half past eight, and you are not ill enough to stay home and not well enough to pretend nothing is happening. Somebody asks how you are. The honest answer is a degree rather than a state, and reporting it without asking anybody to do something about it is exactly what this word is for.
setting.jp: ちょっと風邪気味です。
setting.en: I've got a bit of a cold coming on.

extensions.scene: You use it about tiredness rather than illness later the same week, which is the other place it lives and the one where it does most of its social work.
extensions.jp: 最近、疲れ気味です。
extensions.en: I've been a touch tired lately.

extensions.t: It is a degree, not a frequency — that is がち's job. 遅れ気味 means running slightly late today; 遅れがち means late a lot, as a habit. About a colleague the difference is between a Tuesday and a character reference.
extensions.scene: You use the wrong one about somebody else and turn a single late morning into a standing accusation, which is a much larger thing to have said than you meant to say.
extensions.jp: 遅れがちです。
extensions.en: Late a lot — a habit, and a much bigger thing to say.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: The flat is small, it is above a bakery, and the rent is a third less than the one you looked at on Tuesday. Somebody asks whether it is any good, and the honest answer is not good or bad — it is good for what it costs, which needs a benchmark inside the sentence.
setting.jp: 値段のわりに、おいしいです。
setting.en: For the price, it's good.

extensions.scene: You use it about a person rather than a thing, which is where it is most common and most useful — and where the benchmark being undercut is somebody's age rather than a price.
extensions.jp: 若いわりに、しっかりしています。
extensions.en: For someone so young, he's very together.

extensions.t: The two halves have to genuinely disagree. A pairing that is not surprising reads as a clumsy comparison, because the pattern promises a gap and the listener waits for one — 安いわりに安い is not a sentence anybody finishes.
extensions.scene: You use it in a sentence where the two halves agree rather than disagree, and the listener pauses, still waiting for the second shoe that the pattern promised and the sentence never actually dropped.
extensions.jp: 高いわりに、おいしくないです。
extensions.en: Expensive, and not even good — the gap the pattern promises.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Four months into a study habit and the odd thing has started happening: the more you read, the less certain you feel, because every page shows you two more things you did not know. Saying that needs a frame that scales one thing against another, and both halves use the same verb.
setting.jp: 練習すればするほど、上手になります。
setting.en: The more you practise, the better you get.

extensions.scene: You use the version that is actually true of your week, where the slope runs downhill rather than up, and the frame turns out to carry discouragement exactly as well as it carries progress.
extensions.jp: 考えれば考えるほど、わからなくなります。
extensions.en: The more I think about it, the less I understand.

extensions.t: The verb must be the same on both sides. 読めば書くほど is not a scale, it is two unrelated things bolted together, and the sentence collapses. And the ば-form is Step 16's — this pattern is a large part of why that lesson mattered.
extensions.scene: You try it with two different verbs and the frame stops meaning anything at all, because a scale needs the same thing on both ends and two unrelated verbs are not a scale.
extensions.jp: 高ければ高いほどいいです。
extensions.en: The pricier the better — adjectives take ければ〜いほど.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Somebody says your Japanese must be almost fluent by now. They mean it kindly, they have heard you order lunch, and it is not remotely close to true. A polite correction would understate how far off it is — and there is a word for overturning an assumption rather than gently adjusting it.
setting.jp: 安いどころか、とても高かったです。
setting.en: Far from cheap — it was very expensive.

extensions.scene: You use it about a holiday that was supposed to be restful and was not, where the assumption and the reality point in genuinely opposite directions rather than merely differing by a degree or two.
extensions.jp: 休むどころか、もっと忙しくなりました。
extensions.en: Far from resting, I got busier.

extensions.t: It is not a soft correction. どころか says the assumption was not merely wrong but backwards, so aimed at somebody else's claim it reads as contradiction — about yourself it is safe, and often modest.
extensions.scene: You aim it at a colleague's estimate rather than your own and it lands harder than the room expected, because overturning somebody else's claim is a different act from overturning your own.
extensions.jp: 思ったより高かったです。
extensions.en: Pricier than I expected — the soft version, for somebody else's claim.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Six words that all do something English handles with adverbs and a raised eyebrow: they grade a claim instead of stating one. Met separately they look like vocabulary and get used interchangeably. Together they are the difference between a sentence that reports something and a sentence that takes a position on it.
setting.jp: 忘れがち
setting.en: Often — a tendency, and an unwelcome one.

extensions.scene: You rewrite a flat paragraph of adjectives using three of them, and it stops sounding like a list and starts sounding like an opinion — which is the whole difference this step is for.
extensions.jp: 値段のわりに、いいです。
extensions.en: Good for the price — a benchmark, not an adjective.

extensions.t: The commonest error is がち for 気味 and back. One is how often and the other is how much, and about a person that is the difference between describing their week and describing them.
extensions.scene: You check each one against the question it actually answers — how often, or how much — and the pair that kept collapsing into each other separates immediately and stays separated.
extensions.jp: 疲れ気味です。
extensions.en: A touch tired — a degree, today.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A handover note from somebody who has left, with six steps on it, and a system that will do something expensive if the steps happen in the wrong order. When you report back that it is done, the word you want claims precision rather than approximation.
setting.jp: 言ったとおりにやりました。
setting.en: I did it exactly as you said.

extensions.scene: You use the voiced version, which is nearly a fixed expression by now and is one of the two or three most useful short answers in any Japanese working week.
extensions.jp: 会議は予定どおり始まりました。
extensions.en: The meeting started on schedule.

extensions.t: It is not ような. ような is like, resembling; とおり is exactly as, following. 言ったようにやりました is I did it more or less as you said, which is a weaker promise than anybody wants on a handover.
extensions.scene: You use the softer one by accident and end up promising rather less than you actually delivered, which on a handover note is a strange and slightly costly direction in which to get something wrong.
extensions.jp: 説明のとおりにやりました。
extensions.en: Exactly as explained — no room left in it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: On the train, somebody two seats down is having a phone conversation that everybody can hear and nobody wants to be part of. The entire carriage is doing the same thing, and there is a word for it that makes the pretending itself the action.
setting.jp: 彼は知らないふりをしました。
setting.en: He pretended not to know.

extensions.scene: You use it about yourself and a colleague's very obvious new haircut, where the pretending was clearly the kind thing to do rather than the dishonest one, and everybody at the table was doing it.
extensions.jp: 気づかないふりをしました。
extensions.en: I pretended not to notice.

extensions.t: It carries a judgement, usually mild. Saying somebody 知らないふりをした accuses them of a small dishonesty — so it is not the neutral way to report that they did not know, which is simply 知りませんでした.
extensions.scene: You use it where the person genuinely had no idea, and accidentally accuse them of a small dishonesty they did not commit — the judgement is inside the word and cannot be removed by tone.
extensions.jp: 知りませんでした。
extensions.en: He didn't know — no pretence claimed.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A reflective paragraph in a year-end report, about a decision you knew at the time was the wrong one and made anyway. Two things true of the same person at the same moment, and they contradict each other — which is a shape Step 7's ながら could hold the timing of but not the contradiction.
setting.jp: 知っていながらも、何も言いませんでした。
setting.en: Even knowing, I said nothing.

extensions.scene: You use the adjective version about the small office you are describing, where the concession is much gentler and the sentence turns out to be a compliment rather than an admission of anything.
extensions.jp: 小さいながらも、いい店です。
extensions.en: Small though it is, it's a good shop.

extensions.t: Do not confuse it with plain ながら. 音楽を聞きながら勉強する is two compatible actions in one body; 知っていながら言わなかった is two incompatible ones, and the も is what makes the difference audible.
extensions.scene: You drop the も and the sentence stops conceding anything at all — it simply describes two things happening at once, which was Step 7's job and not this one's.
extensions.jp: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
extensions.en: Two compatible actions — plain ながら, no contradiction.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: A line in a drama that the subtitles render as even though, said by one character to another, and the temperature of the room changes. The subtitle is not wrong and it is not close to enough — the word carries contempt, and a learner who files it beside のに will one day use it and not understand what happened.
setting.jp: 知っているくせに、教えてくれませんでした。
setting.en: He knew perfectly well, and still wouldn't tell me.

extensions.scene: You look for the neutral version of the same sentence and find it two steps back, in Step 21, where it has been sitting the whole time doing the job without the contempt.
extensions.jp: 知っているのに、教えてくれませんでした。
extensions.en: He knew, and still wouldn't tell me — のに, with no sneer.

extensions.t: ⚠️ This is genuinely insulting and です does not soften it. 子どものくせに is not affectionate — it means you are only a child, so how dare you. Recognise it in fiction and in arguments; for a neutral even though use のに, and for a polite one けど.
extensions.scene: You hear it used affectionately between two close friends and realise the exception proves how sharp the default is — it works there because both of them know it should not.
extensions.jp: 高いけど、買います。
extensions.en: Expensive, but I'm buying it — the safe one, always.

flags: ⚠️ RUDENESS FLAG, same treatment as meirei: くせに is genuinely contemptuous and a learner meeting it in a drama will misjudge how it lands. The lesson says so explicitly.
No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: You sit down for the first time since seven in the morning, and the phone rings. Not a minute later — at the exact moment your weight reaches the chair, as though the two events were connected, which they were not. There is a pattern for that seam and the surprise is built into it.
setting.jp: 座ったとたん、電話が鳴りました。
setting.en: The instant I sat down, the phone rang.

extensions.scene: You use it about the weather, which is where most people meet it first and where the timing is at its most unfair — the rain waiting, apparently, for the door to close behind you.
extensions.jp: 外に出たとたん、雨が降りはじめました。
extensions.en: The moment I stepped outside, it started raining.

extensions.t: It cannot carry your own intention. 家を出たとたん、買い物に行きました is wrong — you cannot plan the thing that happens at the instant, and if the second half is something you chose, the sentence wants てから or たら instead.
extensions.scene: You write one where the second half was your own decision and the pattern quietly stops working, because a seam is something that happens to you rather than something you arrange.
extensions.jp: 家を出てから、買い物に行きました。
extensions.en: After leaving, I went shopping — chosen, so てから.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Nine minutes into a meeting that took three weeks to arrange, with everybody finally in the room, a phone goes off. Not during the meeting in the general sense — in the thick of it, at the worst available moment, which is a finer claim than Step 19's neutral window.
setting.jp: 会議の最中に、電話が鳴りました。
setting.en: The phone rang right in the middle of the meeting.

extensions.scene: You use it about a conversation rather than a meeting, where the interruption is somebody walking away rather than a noise, and the thing being broken into is your own half-finished sentence.
extensions.jp: 話している最中に、帰ってしまいました。
extensions.en: He left while I was still talking.

extensions.t: It needs an activity with a middle. 寝ている最中に is odd for ordinary sleep, because sleeping is not an activity underway the way a meeting is — 寝ている間に is the natural sentence there, and 間に is the neutral window this one intensifies.
extensions.scene: You try it about ordinary sleep and it is subtly wrong in a way the neutral window is not, because sleeping is not an activity underway the way a meeting is.
extensions.jp: 寝ている間に、電話がありました。
extensions.en: While I slept, a call came — the neutral window.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: An email you have to send before you leave, about a decision that has not been made yet, to somebody who needs to know the moment it is. Not when it is decided, not after — as soon as, and the sentence is a promise rather than a description.
setting.jp: 決まり次第、ご連絡します。
setting.en: I'll be in touch as soon as it's decided.

extensions.scene: You use it in the room rather than in writing, to start something the moment the last person arrives, and it is the same promise made out loud instead of on paper.
extensions.jp: 到着次第、始めましょう。
extensions.en: Let's start as soon as everyone's here.

extensions.t: It cannot be used about the past, because the pattern is a promise — 決まり次第連絡しました is not a sentence. And the second half must be something you control: 決まり次第、雨が降ります is nonsense for exactly the same reason.
extensions.scene: You try to report a past sequence with it and the tense restriction refuses outright, which is the fastest way to learn that this pattern is a promise rather than a description.
extensions.jp: 決まってから、連絡しました。
extensions.en: After it was decided, I got in touch — past, so てから.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Three patterns that all come out in English as when or as soon as, and all mean something different about where in an event you are standing. Side by side the difference stops being subtle, and the tense restrictions do most of the work of telling them apart.
setting.jp: 座ったとたん、電話が鳴りました。
setting.en: The seam — past, and a surprise you did not control.

extensions.scene: You sort three sentences from your own week into the three grains, and two of them turn out to have wanted a different one from the one you used at the time.
extensions.jp: 決まり次第、ご連絡します。
extensions.en: As soon as possible — future, and your own promise.

extensions.t: The tense restrictions are absolute and they are the fastest self-check there is: たとたん is past and uncontrolled, 次第 is future and controlled. If a sentence wants both at once, it wants neither of them.
extensions.scene: You test a sentence against both restrictions and it fails each of them, which is how you find out it never wanted any of the three and had wanted てから all along.
extensions.jp: 会議の最中に、電話が鳴りました。
extensions.en: The thick of it — an activity interrupted.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9 runs on N3 vocabulary, so kanji outside KANJI_DICT is the norm rather than the exception here — furigana needed throughout the stage. Flagged once per lesson rather than once per line.

setting.scene: Your residence card renewal is finally in, and the clerk has just talked you through three forms at a speed built for people who grew up here. You need all of it again. Every request you own ends in てください, and in the half-second before you speak you can feel that telling this man to explain it a second time is not the thing you want to be doing.
setting.jp: もう一度説明してください。
setting.en: Please explain that once more — correct, and still an instruction.

extensions.scene: Pointed upward, a request stops being an instruction and becomes a question about what you might receive. The verb is Step 14's いただく, moved into the potential: could I receive the favour of your explaining it. Nothing in the content changed. The sentence simply stopped telling him anything.
extensions.jp: もう一度説明していただけますか。
extensions.en: Could you explain that once more?

extensions.scene: The potential is not decoration. Take it out and the sentence announces that you are about to receive an explanation, which is an odd thing to say to a man who has not offered one yet, and he will hear the difference before you finish saying it.
extensions.jp: 説明していただきますか
extensions.en: Not a request — an announcement with a question mark on it.

extensions.scene: The same shape aimed sideways overshoots instead. Asking the colleague at the next desk for a hand with いただけますか opens a distance neither of you wanted, and もらえますか was already the right height for somebody standing level with you.
extensions.jp: 手伝ってもらえますか。
extensions.en: Could you give me a hand? — level, and correct there.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: The counter at the bank has your form and a problem with it. You have been waiting eleven minutes and are plainly about to wait more, and the woman behind the glass says a sentence you have heard a thousand times in this country without once being told how it is put together or that you could build one yourself.
setting.jp: 少々お待ちください。
setting.en: One moment please — heard daily, never parsed.

extensions.scene: Now put it in your own mouth, asking rather than telling. Swap ください for いただけますか and the identical frame stops instructing and starts requesting, which is what you need the moment the person being asked to wait is the one above you.
extensions.jp: 少々お待ちいただけますか。
extensions.en: Could you wait a moment? — the frame, asking.

extensions.scene: The common overbuild is to put する back in. ご確認していただけますか sounds like somebody being careful, and it is exactly one part too many — the frame already contains the verb, so the extra して has nothing to do but announce the effort.
extensions.jp: ご確認していただけますか
extensions.en: One part too many — the frame already holds the verb.

extensions.scene: And the same frame with になる instead points the benefit the other way. お待ちになりますか asks whether they intend to wait; お待ちいただけますか asks them to wait for you. Same person elevated, opposite thing being said.
extensions.jp: お待ちになりますか。
extensions.en: Are you going to wait? — polite, and not a request.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You need Thursday off. In English the message writes itself in six words. In Japanese every shape you own says either 休みます, which is flat and states a fact at a man who outranks you, or 休んでもいいですか, which is Step 5 asking permission the way a schoolchild asks to leave the room. Neither is what an adult sends a section chief.
setting.jp: 木曜日は休みます。
setting.en: I'm taking Thursday off — true, flat, and faintly rude.

extensions.scene: The adult form is built out of two things already in your hands. Step 20's causative turns 休む into being-let-to-rest; Step 14's いただく receives that permission humbly. The decision is still entirely yours. The sentence hands him the credit for it.
extensions.jp: 木曜日は休ませていただきます。
extensions.en: I'll be taking Thursday off — permission, granted to itself.

extensions.scene: Somebody's permission has to be plausibly involved or the humility attaches to nothing. Said about your own coffee in your own kitchen with nobody else in the building, it is a joke, and it is the joke Japanese speakers make about the form most often.
extensions.jp: コーヒーを飲ませていただきます
extensions.en: Nobody permitted this. Empty politeness, and audibly so.

extensions.scene: Move to the potential and the announcement turns into a question. 使わせていただきます takes the thing and tells you afterwards; 使わせていただけますか asks first, and standing at a counter that difference is the entire exchange.
extensions.jp: こちらを使わせていただけますか。
extensions.en: May I use this? — asked, not announced.

claims: The Japanese government's keigo guidelines address 〜させていただく directly, as a construction people ask about and overreach with.
sources: 敬語の指針, 文化審議会答申, 2 February 2007 (平成19年) — https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkashingikai/kokugo/hokoku/pdf/keigo_tosin.pdf
flags: Stage 3 necessarily uses keigo vocabulary outside KANJI_DICT (申・参・召・覧・尊敬語・謙譲語 and the like). Furigana needed throughout this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

The claim about the 2007 guidelines is cited to the 答申 itself. A reviewer should confirm the characterisation — that the document treats させていただく as a point of overreach rather than merely listing it — before this ships.

setting.scene: One pen, one day. You want to borrow it at breakfast from the flatmate, at eleven from the colleague at the next desk, and at two in the afternoon from the man behind the ward office counter who has never seen you before and never will again. Same pen, same want, three different sentences, and the difference is not politeness. It is distance.
setting.jp: ペン、貸して。
setting.en: Lend us a pen — a friend, and nothing is missing from it.

extensions.scene: So climb. もらえますか for the colleague, いただけますか for anybody above you, お貸しいただけないでしょうか for the stranger who owes you nothing at all. Five rungs out of one verb, and the rung is picked by who is standing there rather than by how badly you want the pen.
extensions.jp: ペンをお貸しいただけないでしょうか。
extensions.en: Might I trouble you for a pen? — the top rung.

extensions.scene: Too high is not the safe error. The top rung aimed at the flatmate over breakfast lands as sarcasm or as a grievance, and either way you spend the next minute explaining that nothing is wrong, which is worse than the borrowing was.
extensions.jp: お貸しいただけないでしょうか。
extensions.en: To a friend: a joke, or a complaint. Not politeness.

extensions.scene: Pick the rung once and then hold it. Climbing halfway through a conversation is far more audible than starting one rung low and staying put, because the climb tells the other person you have just this second reassessed who they are.
extensions.jp: ペンを貸してもらえますか。
extensions.en: Rung three — a colleague, level with you.

The five-rung ordering is the author's calibration, not a cited one. This is the item in the step most in need of a native speaker saying where the rungs actually sit.

setting.scene: A colleague forwards you a message and asks what it says. You can read every word in it and you still cannot answer, because the answer is not any of the sentences — it is the thing all of them add up to, and your Japanese so far has only ever let you repeat sentences rather than summarise them.
setting.jp: 田中さんは来られません。
setting.en: Tanaka can't come — one sentence, faithfully repeated.

extensions.scene: Package the whole clause instead of echoing it. ということだ hands the content over as a report you are relaying rather than a claim you are making, which is exactly the position a person forwarding a message is in.
extensions.jp: 田中さんは来られないということです。
extensions.en: The message says Tanaka can't come.

extensions.scene: The same shape does a second job. Put つまり in front and it stops reporting and starts summarising — three paragraphs compressed into the one sentence that survives them. It is the shape a summary arrives in, and it is what somebody wants when they ask you what a long message actually said.
extensions.jp: つまり、会議は中止ということです。
extensions.en: So the upshot is: the meeting is off.
extensions.t: ということ packages a whole clause into a noun. Reporting and summarising are the same move — handing over content without owning it.

setting.scene: You are twenty minutes into a conversation with a neighbour and it has run dry. She mentions that her daughter has moved to Kyoto. In English you would say oh, Kyoto, and coast into a new subject on the strength of it, and in Japanese you have no idea how to make that turn without it sounding like an interruption.
setting.jp: 京都はいいところですね。
setting.en: Kyoto's a nice place — true, and it ends the topic.

extensions.scene: というと picks the word up out of what she just said and hands it back as the new subject. The conversation changes direction and nobody has to announce that it did, which is the whole trick.
extensions.jp: 京都というと、お寺ですね。
extensions.en: Speaking of Kyoto — temples, right?

extensions.scene: It also works on yourself. Say something, then pick up your own word to go somewhere with it — the standard way a story gets from one part to the next without a visible seam.
extensions.jp: 夏というと、花火を思い出します。
extensions.en: Summer makes me think of fireworks.
extensions.t: といえば is interchangeable in speech. Both need something already said to pick up; neither can open a conversation.

setting.scene: You are reading a Japanese page about a word you do not know, having finally given up on English dictionaries because they keep giving you a synonym rather than a meaning. The definition begins with the word itself, then six characters you have seen a thousand times and never parsed as a unit, and then the actual explanation.
setting.jp: 「謎」は説明できないことです。
setting.en: A mystery is something inexplicable — correct, and blunt.

extensions.scene: というのは is the frame a definition arrives in. It marks what follows as an explanation of the word rather than a statement about the world, which is why every dictionary entry and every patient teacher uses it.
extensions.jp: 「謎」というのは、説明できないことです。
extensions.en: A mystery is something that cannot be explained.

extensions.scene: The same frame does a second, stranger job: giving a reason AFTER the claim, in a sentence of its own. English puts because in front; this puts it behind, and a learner reading top to bottom keeps missing it.
extensions.jp: 肉は食べません。というのは、菜食主義だからです。
extensions.en: I don't eat meat. The reason is that I'm vegetarian.
extensions.t: Definition, reason, and emphasis — three jobs. Its casual form って is what you will actually hear: それってどういう意味。

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody asks how the weather is where you are and you say 涼しいです, cool, and then immediately regret it, because it is not cool, it is properly cold and you have just given them the wrong idea about whether to bring a coat. In English you would say well, cold really, and correct yourself in the same breath.
setting.jp: 今日は涼しいです。
setting.en: Today is cool — and it is not, quite.

extensions.scene: というより replaces the word rather than the fact. You keep the subject, drop the label you reached for, and put the truer one in its place, all inside one sentence and without admitting error.
extensions.jp: 今日は涼しいというより寒いです。
extensions.en: Today is cold rather than cool.

extensions.scene: It is also how you disagree with somebody's description of a thing without telling them they are wrong — you correct the word they chose and leave the person out of it.
extensions.jp: 趣味というより、仕事です。
extensions.en: It's work rather than a hobby.
extensions.t: Step 3's より compares two things. というより replaces one description of one thing. Two items versus two words.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You mention you went away at the weekend and the person's face lights up — where did you go, how long, was it wonderful. It was one night, forty minutes down the line, and you slept badly. In Japanese the word 旅行 has just done far more work than you meant it to, and now you have to walk it back without seeming falsely modest.
setting.jp: 旅行に行きました。
setting.en: I went on a trip — technically true, and oversized.

extensions.scene: といっても shrinks the word you just used, immediately, before the other person builds anything on it. The first half stays true; the second half tells them how small the true thing is.
extensions.jp: 旅行といっても、二日だけです。
extensions.en: A trip — though only two days.

extensions.scene: It is the standard machinery of Japanese modesty, and it runs on almost anything you might be complimented for: your cooking, your Japanese, your job, the flat. The word you used stays true; you are only telling them how much of it there was before they build a question on top of it.
extensions.jp: 料理といっても、卵を焼いただけです。
extensions.en: I say cooking; I fried an egg.
extensions.t: It deflates, it does not contradict. The second half has to leave the first half true and merely smaller.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You are half a page into something written for adults and という has appeared four times. You know the word. You have known it since Step 11. And each of the four is doing something different, and the sentences are coming apart in your hands because you keep assuming the first meaning and reading on.
setting.jp: 田中という人に会いました。
setting.en: I met a person called Tanaka — the one meaning you already had.

extensions.scene: The family sorts itself the moment you stop reading という and start reading what comes AFTER it. こと packages, と picks up, のは defines, より corrects, ても deflates. The stem never changes; the particle is the whole signal.
extensions.jp: 行けないということです。
extensions.en: Packaging a clause — the upshot is he can't go.

extensions.scene: Which means the fix is a listening habit rather than a memorised table: hear という, wait one more beat, and the next syllable tells you which of the five you are in.
extensions.jp: 京都というと、お寺ですね。
extensions.en: Picking up a topic — the same three characters again.
extensions.t: The failure at speed is not producing the wrong member but HEARING the wrong one, and the correction arrives two syllables later.

setting.scene: There is a typhoon somewhere south and everybody at work has an opinion about whether the trains will run. You looked at the forecast this morning and you would like to say so, but every sentence you own states things as facts, and you do not want to be the person who promised the trains would stop.
setting.jp: 明日は雨です。
setting.en: It'll rain tomorrow — asserted, and you have just taken responsibility for it.

extensions.scene: によると puts the source in front and makes you the pipe rather than the origin. What follows is the forecast's claim, not yours, and the sentence closes with そうです to keep it that way.
extensions.jp: 天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうです。
extensions.en: According to the forecast, it'll rain tomorrow.

extensions.scene: The opening and the ending are a pair. によると at the front commits you to a reporting ending — そうです, ということです, らしいです — and a plain です at the end quietly takes the ownership back.
extensions.jp: 新聞によれば、値段が上がるということです。
extensions.en: According to the paper, prices are going up.
extensions.t: Stage 9's によって is the same characters, different job. A REPORT follows によると; a result or a means follows によって.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You are filling in a form at a city office and there is a box asking for anything you want to add about your application. You write 申請について and the clerk, kindly, points at it and says something you half-catch about it being fine but a little casual — and you realise the register of a form is not the register of a conversation.
setting.jp: 申請について書きました。
setting.en: I wrote about the application — correct, and underdressed.

extensions.scene: に関して is について wearing the formal register. Same relation, higher shelf, and it is what appears in a subject line, at the head of a paragraph and on any document somebody will file.
extensions.jp: 申請に関して、質問があります。
extensions.en: I have a question concerning the application.

extensions.scene: Before a NOUN it changes shape to に関する, and this is the half learners drop. 事故に関して記事 is broken; the noun wants the する form in front of it. Learners drop the する form because English does not change shape before a noun, and the error survives into otherwise careful writing.
extensions.jp: 事故に関する記事を読みました。
extensions.en: I read an article concerning the accident.
extensions.t: する before a noun, して before a verb. The same split you already make with として.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Somebody who knew you when you arrived says your Japanese has come on. You want to agree without boasting, and the honest version is not that you are good — it is that the distance between now and your first month is large. Japanese has a shape for exactly that and より is not it.
setting.jp: 今、日本語が上手です。
setting.en: My Japanese is good now — a claim you would rather not make.

extensions.scene: に比べて puts the old state behind the sentence as a reference point and measures the gap instead of picking a winner. It says how far, which is the modest and the accurate thing at once.
extensions.jp: 去年に比べて、上手になりました。
extensions.en: I've got better compared with last year.

extensions.scene: It works on anything with a before and an after — prices, weather, a city, a crowd — and it is the default shape for any observation about change in writing.
extensions.jp: 東京に比べると、ここは静かです。
extensions.en: Compared with Tokyo, it's quiet here.
extensions.t: より puts two items side by side and picks one. に比べて sets one behind as a baseline and sizes the difference.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: It is early October and the light has been going earlier every evening for weeks. You want to say so — not that it got dark, which is a fact about tonight, but that the two things have been moving together all month — and every tool you have describes one moment at a time.
setting.jp: 秋になりました。日が短いです。
setting.en: Autumn came. The days are short. — two facts, no link.

extensions.scene: につれて ties two changes together and makes them travel in step. Neither half causes the other exactly; they simply move at the same time, and one word carries that relation.
extensions.jp: 秋が進むにつれて、日が短くなります。
extensions.en: As autumn advances, the days grow shorter.

extensions.scene: It needs both halves to be genuine changes, so a one-off event breaks it. Arriving happens once and cannot be gradual; approaching has a middle, and a middle is what this pattern is about.
extensions.jp: 年を取るにつれて、時間が早く感じます。
extensions.en: As you get older, time feels faster.
extensions.t: Ask whether the thing has a middle. If it happens all at once, this is the wrong pattern and たら or と is the right one.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The forecast on the platform screen says rain, and it gives two times, and neither of them is a time exactly — it is talking about tonight sliding into tomorrow, and it uses a shape where you were expecting から and まで. You have known から and まで since Step 3 and they have never once looked like this.
setting.jp: 今夜から明日まで雨です。
setting.en: Rain from tonight until tomorrow — exact, and falsely so.

extensions.scene: から〜にかけて gives a range with soft edges. Nobody knows the minute the rain stops, and まで claims that somebody does; にかけて admits the boundary is a smear and reports the stretch honestly.
extensions.jp: 今夜から明日にかけて、雨が降るでしょう。
extensions.en: Rain from tonight through tomorrow.

extensions.scene: The same softness works over places as well as time, which is why weather maps and regional news are built out of it almost exclusively. A weather map is almost entirely built from it, because almost nothing about weather has an edge anybody could name to the minute.
extensions.jp: 北海道から東北にかけて、雪が多いです。
extensions.en: Heavy snow from Hokkaido across the northeast.
extensions.t: If you could not name the minute or the boundary where it stops, まで overstates and にかけて is the honest one.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You are at a wedding and the speeches have started, and every one of them is built out of words you know arranged in a way you do not. Somebody says と共に and you hear the と and expect a list of people, and then the sentence goes somewhere else entirely and you lose the rest of it.
setting.jp: 家族と一緒に暮らしています。
setting.en: I live with my family — ordinary, spoken, and right for a conversation.

extensions.scene: と共に is the same with, in the register a speech is made in. Nothing about the meaning changes; the altitude does, and ceremonial Japanese lives almost entirely up here. Nothing about the meaning has moved at all; only the altitude has, and ceremonial Japanese lives up here almost exclusively.
extensions.jp: 家族と共に暮らしています。
extensions.en: I live together with my family — formal register.

extensions.scene: It has a second job that catches learners out: two things changing at once, doing につれて's work at a higher shelf. Hearing と and expecting a list is exactly what goes wrong.
extensions.jp: 技術の進歩と共に、生活が変わりました。
extensions.en: Life changed along with advances in technology.
extensions.t: For the everyday with, と or と一緒に is what a person says. と共に in casual speech is dressed for an occasion that is not happening.

setting.scene: You sit down to write four sentences about how the neighbourhood has changed and you stall on the first one, because English would let you say about, according to and compared to almost interchangeably and Japanese is asking you to decide, before you can build the sentence, what relation the noun actually bears to the claim.
setting.jp: この町は変わりました。
setting.en: The town has changed — true, and it relates to nothing.

extensions.scene: Each pattern names one relation and only that one. Source, topic, baseline, proportion, range, accompaniment — six relations, six shapes, and English marks almost none of them, which is why the sorting has to be done deliberately once.
extensions.jp: 調査によると、人口が減っているそうです。
extensions.en: Source — the survey says so, and I do not.

extensions.scene: The two that cross most often share their characters. によると is followed by a report; によって is followed by a result or a means. What comes AFTER settles it, every time.
extensions.jp: 去年に比べて、店が減りました。
extensions.en: Baseline — measured against last year.
extensions.t: Source によると · topic について / に関して · baseline に比べて · proportion につれて · range から〜にかけて · accompaniment と共に.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You have to write two lines thanking a group of people, and there is a hierarchy in the room that everybody except you can see. Listing everyone flattens it, which is wrong. Naming only the senior person ignores the rest, which is worse. English would say and everyone else and get away with it.
setting.jp: 皆様に感謝します。
setting.en: My thanks to everyone — safe, and it names nobody.

extensions.scene: をはじめ names the leading member and lets that one stand at the head of the rest. The list admits it is not finishing, and the ranking is carried by the grammar instead of by you.
extensions.jp: 社長をはじめとする皆様に感謝します。
extensions.en: My thanks to the president and to everyone else.

extensions.scene: Outside of thanks it does the same job for places and things — one example that genuinely leads, and the unstated rest behind it. The unstated remainder is doing real work — it says the list could go on, and that you know it, and that you chose not to.
extensions.jp: 東京をはじめ、大都市では家賃が高いです。
extensions.en: Rents are high in Tokyo and other big cities.
extensions.t: The named one must genuinely lead. A minor member in that slot reads as a misjudgement of rank, which in a written notice is a real error.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody asks who uses the app you are describing and the honest answer is not everybody and not only young people either — it is that the weight of it sits with the young and thins out from there. You can say 若い人が使います, which is true and implies nobody else does.
setting.jp: 若い人が使っています。
setting.en: Young people use it — true, and it shuts the door on everyone else.

extensions.scene: を中心に names a centre of gravity rather than a boundary. It says where most of the thing is and leaves the edges open, which is what an honest description of any distribution needs.
extensions.jp: 若い人を中心に使われています。
extensions.en: It's used mainly by younger people.

extensions.scene: The centre can be a place, a topic or a person, and the pattern is the standard way any spread, any syllabus and any campaign gets described. It is how any spread gets described honestly: naming where the mass sits without pretending to know where it stops.
extensions.jp: 文法を中心に勉強しています。
extensions.en: I'm studying with grammar at the centre of it.
extensions.t: をはじめ names a leading MEMBER. を中心に names a FOCUS. One heads a list; the other marks where the mass is.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Your section head is out and a call comes in for him that you have to answer properly. You know how to say he is not here. What you do not know how to say is the next part — that you are speaking in his place, which is the sentence that decides whether the caller keeps talking to you or asks to ring back.
setting.jp: 部長はいません。私が聞きます。
setting.en: He isn't here. I'll listen. — two sentences and no authority.

extensions.scene: にかわって says you are standing in somebody's place. One phrase does what those two sentences failed to do, because it names the role rather than merely the person. What it names is the role rather than the person, which is exactly the information the caller needs in order to decide whether to go on.
extensions.jp: 部長にかわって、私がお伺いします。
extensions.en: I'll take it on the section head's behalf.

extensions.scene: It also covers one thing replacing another over time, which is how any account of change gets written — the letter giving way to the email, the shop to the machine.
extensions.jp: 手紙にかわって、メールが使われています。
extensions.en: Email has taken the place of letters.
extensions.t: Step 43's 代わりに is the ordinary instead of. にかわって is specifically taking somebody's ROLE, and using it for objects claims they had jobs.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You are choosing between two Japanese courses on a website and the descriptions look identical until you notice that one says 初心者向け and the other 初心者向き. One kana apart. You assume it is a typo, pick the cheaper one, and spend six weeks in a class that was never designed for you.
setting.jp: 初心者のコースです。
setting.en: It's a beginners' course — and which kind, exactly.

extensions.scene: 向け means somebody BUILT it for that audience. 向き means it happens to suit them. The difference is intention, and in an advertisement intention is the whole of what is being promised.
extensions.jp: 初心者向けのコースです。
extensions.en: A course designed for beginners.

extensions.scene: 向き also keeps its literal sense of facing, which is where it turns up in every flat listing you will ever read and is the reason south-facing rooms cost more.
extensions.jp: 南向きの部屋がいいです。
extensions.en: I'd like a south-facing room.
extensions.t: Aimed at: 向け. Happens to suit: 向き. Facing: 向き. One kana, and it is on every product description in the country.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: The lavatory door at the station says 使用中 and you can read both characters and you still hesitate, because you have met 中 as inside and this is plainly not that. Two doors down another sign says 準備中 and a third says 営業中, and all three are telling you something about time rather than space.
setting.jp: 使っています。
setting.en: It's in use — the sentence you would build.

extensions.scene: 中 clipped onto a noun says in the middle of, and it will end. It is the shortest possible sign and the country runs on it: 工事中, 会議中, 電話中, 準備中.
extensions.jp: ただいま準備中です。
extensions.en: We're getting ready — the sign on the door.

extensions.scene: The same character read じゅう means the opposite kind of thing: all the way through, with no gaps. Which reading a word takes is a property of the word, not a rule.
extensions.jp: 一日中、雨が降っていました。
extensions.en: It rained all day long.
extensions.t: ちゅう is a middle that ends. じゅう is a span with no gaps. There is no shortcut for which; it is learned per word.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You are fifteen minutes late and the reason is boring and real — you stopped for bread. The explanation you can build makes it sound like you went out to buy bread and happened to arrive afterwards, which makes you sound like somebody who prioritised bread.
setting.jp: パンを買いました。それから来ました。
setting.en: I bought bread. Then I came. — accurate, and damning.

extensions.scene: 途中で puts the bread on the way to something else. The journey stays the main clause and the errand becomes a thing that happened during it, which is both truer and considerably better for you.
extensions.jp: 来る途中で、パンを買いました。
extensions.en: I bought bread on the way here.

extensions.scene: It covers being part way through an action as well as part way along a road, which is how most interruptions get described. The interruption becomes a thing that happened inside the meeting rather than an event that replaced it, which is both truer and kinder to everyone.
extensions.jp: 会議の途中で、電話が鳴りました。
extensions.en: The phone rang part way through the meeting.
extensions.t: Stage 9's 最中に is the dramatic version, and it resents the interruption. 途中で is neutral and reports a position.
