setting.scene: You read a notice on a noticeboard three times. Every word is one you know. And you still cannot tell whether the thing described is for you, whether it is happening now or all month, or whether it has already finished — because all of that information is carried by suffixes that English would have spelled out in a clause.
setting.jp: お知らせがあります。
setting.en: There's a notice — and you cannot decode it.

extensions.scene: Every pattern in this step marks SCOPE: who a thing is for, whether anybody meant it that way, who is standing in for whom, and how much of a period or a place is covered. English marks almost none of it explicitly.
extensions.jp: 初心者向けの教室を、来月中に開きます。
extensions.en: A class for beginners, opening at some point next month.

extensions.scene: Which is why this step raises what you can READ faster than what you can say — and at this stage that is the correct trade, because the reading is where you are actually stuck.
extensions.jp: 若い人を中心に、工事中の道を避けています。
extensions.en: Younger people especially are avoiding the road that's under construction.
extensions.t: Leading member をはじめ · focus を中心に · substitution にかわって · suited 向き · aimed at 向け · in the middle ちゅう / 途中で · all through じゅう.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: The line has stopped, the announcement says an hour, and the hotel is three kilometres away in the rain. There is no decision left to make and you would like to say so out loud to the person beside you, but every sentence you own about necessity sounds like you are quoting a rule at them.
setting.jp: 歩かなければなりません。
setting.en: We have to walk — as though a regulation said so.

extensions.scene: しかない says the options ran out rather than that a rule applies. It is resignation with a grammar behind it, and it is how adults actually announce that a decision has been made for them.
extensions.jp: 歩くしかないですね。
extensions.en: Nothing for it but to walk.

extensions.scene: Because the resignation is in the word, your voice does not have to carry it — which is what makes it usable about your own situation without sounding like a complaint.
extensions.jp: 待つしかありません。
extensions.en: There's nothing to do but wait.
extensions.t: Step 5's なければならない is a rule requiring it. しかない is the alternatives running out. Using it about a regulation sounds like complaining about weather.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You are standing at a ticket machine you have used twice before and cannot remember which button comes first, and there is a queue. You need the shortest possible question, and the one you have — 何をしますか — asks what somebody is doing rather than what you should do.
setting.jp: どうしますか。
setting.en: What will you do? — asked of the machine, apparently.

extensions.scene: どうすればいいですか is the sentence. Step 16's ば gave the conditional; いい on the end turns it into what would be good if I did — a request for advice rather than a report of confusion.
extensions.jp: どうすればいいですか。
extensions.en: What should I do?

extensions.scene: The answer comes back in the same shape, and it is the shape of every simple instruction you will be given in Japan: this one thing, and you are done.
extensions.jp: ボタンを押せばいいです。
extensions.en: You just have to press the button.
extensions.t: It shrinks a problem to one action, which is why it reassures. On a genuinely hard problem it can read as dismissive.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You are explaining why you have not been to a place everybody assumes you must have visited, and the reason is not money or interest — it is one thing, time, and if that single condition were met the whole rest of it would follow. English has if only for this and you have been building it out of もし and から.
setting.jp: 時間がないから、行きません。
setting.en: I don't go because I've no time — a reason, flatly given.

extensions.scene: さえ〜ば reduces the whole problem to one sufficient condition. Not among the reasons — THE reason, and everything else is already in place behind it. Everything else is already in place behind it, and saying so is what separates a reason from an excuse.
extensions.jp: 時間さえあれば、行きたいです。
extensions.en: If only I had the time, I'd go.

extensions.scene: The same word does a second job pointing the other way: picking the most extreme case to prove that the ordinary ones are covered. If the extreme case is covered then the ordinary ones need no arguing, which is why it turns up in arguments far more than in descriptions.
extensions.jp: それは子供でさえ分かります。
extensions.en: Even a child understands that.
extensions.t: も also means even and is far commoner. さえ is stronger and slightly literary — using it where も would do makes a plain sentence argue.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: A student asks you how to get better at something you are good at, and you know the answer, and everything you can build points straight at them — you must, you should, you have to. All of it lands as instruction, and none of it is how the advice was given to you.
setting.jp: 毎日練習しなければなりません。
setting.en: You have to practise daily — an order, however kindly meant.

extensions.scene: ことだ states the advice as a general truth with nobody's name on it. Because it never says you, it arrives as counsel rather than command, which is why teachers live in it.
extensions.jp: 毎日少しずつ練習することです。
extensions.en: The thing is to practise a little every day.

extensions.scene: The negative does the same job for what to avoid, and it is gentler than a prohibition because it still never names the person it is aimed at. It is gentler than a prohibition precisely because it still never names the person it is aimed at, and both of you know that.
extensions.jp: 同じ失敗を繰り返さないことだ。
extensions.en: The thing is not to repeat the same mistake.
extensions.t: It points downward. Said to a superior it reverses the ranks — 早く帰ることです to your boss instructs him from above.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Somebody apologises to you for the fourth time about something that did not matter the first time, and you can hear that they are going to keep going. You want to release them from it, and 大丈夫です has already failed three times because it answers whether you are fine rather than whether they owed you anything.
setting.jp: 大丈夫です。
setting.en: It's fine — said three times now, to no effect.

extensions.scene: ことはない removes the obligation rather than reassuring about the outcome. There was never a reason to apologise, which is a different and much more effective thing to say. There was never a reason to apologise, which is a different and far more effective thing to say than that you are unharmed.
extensions.jp: 謝ることはないですよ。
extensions.en: There's really no need to apologise.

extensions.scene: It works the same way on worry, and it is the natural reply to somebody talking themselves into a state about something that has not happened. It is the natural reply to somebody talking themselves into a state about something that has not happened and probably will not.
extensions.jp: 心配することはありませんよ。
extensions.en: There's no need to worry.
extensions.t: Step 5's なくてもいい permits not doing it. ことはない says there was never a reason to — it removes the obligation rather than waiving it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You are asked whether you can make Saturday. You can, technically, at the cost of the only free morning you have this month, and you do not want to say no outright to somebody who has been kind to you. In English the answer starts well, I could, and everybody understands what that means.
setting.jp: 行けます。
setting.en: I can go — true, and it commits you entirely.

extensions.scene: ないことはない is the double negative that says yes without enthusiasm. The shape itself signals that a reservation is coming, and the listener will wait for it rather than booking you in.
extensions.jp: 行けないことはないですが、遅くなります。
extensions.en: It's not that I can't go, but I'd be late.

extensions.scene: Native listeners read it as a no in progress, which is exactly its value — it lets both people find out where the limit is without either of them having to name it.
extensions.jp: できないこともないけど、時間がかかる。
extensions.en: It's not undoable, but it'd take time.
extensions.t: If you mean an ordinary yes, say the ordinary yes. This shape will be heard as hedging whatever you intended by it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Somebody asks which of two dates suits you and neither is better — you genuinely do not mind, and どちらでもいいです has come out sounding like you cannot be bothered to think about it, which is not what you meant and is how it landed. You would like a way to say that you have no preference which does not sound like you have no interest.
setting.jp: どちらでもいいです。
setting.en: Either's fine — and it can sound like indifference to the asker.

extensions.scene: かまいません says it makes no difference to me rather than either is good. The distinction is what you are claiming: いい approves the options, かまわない declines to have a preference, which is the honest position.
extensions.jp: どちらでもかまいません。
extensions.en: Either is genuinely fine by me.

extensions.scene: The question form asks permission a notch above てもいいですか, and it is the register a request in an office or a waiting room wants. It is the register a request in an office or a waiting room wants, and it is one notch above the form you learned in Step 5.
extensions.jp: 窓を閉めてもかまいませんか。
extensions.en: Would you mind if I closed the window?
extensions.t: Because it means I do not mind, it can read as cold where approval was wanted. To a child showing you a drawing, かまわない is the wrong word.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: A landlord, a form and a colleague have all told you today that something must happen, and they meant three different things by it — a legal requirement, a lack of alternatives, and a strong preference. You answered all three the same way and got a puzzled look from one of them.
setting.jp: しなければなりません。
setting.en: I have to — used for all three, and right for only one.

extensions.scene: There is a dial here, and the rungs are not interchangeable. Forced by rule, forced by circumstance, sufficient, permitted, unnecessary — five positions, and Japanese makes you pick one before you can finish the sentence.
extensions.jp: 電車がないので、歩くしかありません。
extensions.en: No rule involved — the options simply ran out.

extensions.scene: The release end of the dial is the one learners never reach for, and it is the most socially useful: telling somebody that a thing they think they owe you was never owed.
extensions.jp: 心配することはありませんよ。
extensions.en: Released — there was never a reason to.
extensions.t: Rule なければならない · no options しかない · enough ばいい / さえ〜ば · permitted てもかまわない · unnecessary ことはない.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Somebody suggests that a colleague leaked something, and it is not that you doubt it — it is that the person in question was not in the country that week and the suggestion cannot get off the ground. 違います answers a question nobody asked, because the claim is not false so much as impossible.
setting.jp: 違います。
setting.en: That's wrong — a denial of the fact, aimed at the wrong thing.

extensions.scene: わけがない denies that there is any route by which the thing could be true. Stage 9's に違いない said it must be so; this is its exact mirror, and it rejects the possibility rather than the claim.
extensions.jp: 彼が知っているわけがありません。
extensions.en: There's no way he knows.

extensions.scene: It carries force, so it needs somewhere to land. Among people you owe politeness to, はずがない does the same work with the edge taken off. The force is the point, so it needs somewhere to land — among people you owe politeness to, はずがない does the same work with the edge off.
extensions.jp: そんなに安いわけがないでしょう。
extensions.en: There's no way it's that cheap.
extensions.t: Aimed at a person's statement it calls it impossible rather than mistaken. Choose it when you mean that, and はずがない when you do not.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: It is twenty past seven, your work is finished, and everybody else is still at their desks. You are physically able to stand up and go home and you are not going to, and the sentence for that is not できない — you can. You just cannot.
setting.jp: 帰ることができません。
setting.en: I can't go home — which is not true, and everybody knows it.

extensions.scene: わけにはいかない is the grammar for the thing you are able to do and socially cannot. That Japanese has a dedicated form for it tells you how often the situation comes up.
extensions.jp: みんな働いているので、帰るわけにはいきません。
extensions.en: I can't very well leave while everyone's working.

extensions.scene: Negate it and it flips into obligation from the same source: not a rule, but a promise or a relationship that has closed the option off. The obligation comes from a promise or a relationship rather than a regulation, and that is exactly the distinction the pattern exists to mark.
extensions.jp: 約束したので、行かないわけにはいかない。
extensions.en: I promised, so I can't not go.
extensions.t: It needs a SOCIAL reason. 高いから買うわけにはいかない is odd, because money is a plain constraint rather than an obligation.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Somebody says, warmly and with no ill intent, that people from your country all like a particular thing. You do not. You also do not want to make it a confrontation, because they were being friendly, and 違います turns a pleasantry into a correction of them.
setting.jp: いいえ、違います。
setting.en: No, that's wrong — true, and it makes it about them.

extensions.scene: とは限らない denies the ALWAYS while granting the usually. It is the most precise disagreement in the language and the politest, because it leaves the general case standing and takes only the universal claim away.
extensions.jp: みんなが好きだとは限りません。
extensions.en: It's not that everyone likes it.

extensions.scene: 必ずしも in front strengthens it without sharpening it, and the pair is the standard shape for hedging a claim properly in writing. 必ずしも in front strengthens it without sharpening it, and the pair is the standard way a claim gets properly hedged in writing.
extensions.jp: 高いものがいいとは限りません。
extensions.en: Expensive doesn't always mean good.
extensions.t: It attacks the always, not the claim. Using it to mean that is false leaves the listener thinking you half agreed — and proceeding as if you had.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You have been at the desk since seven and the pile has not moved, and somebody asks whether you will finish tonight. You want to say it does not look like it, and the negative you would build from Step 15's そう describes how the pile LOOKS rather than what it is going to do.
setting.jp: 終わりそうじゃないです。
setting.en: It doesn't look that way — a comment on appearances.

extensions.scene: そうもない is the proper negative and it is not the one a learner guesses: the appearance is of it NOT happening. A little despair is built in, which is accurate to the situation.
extensions.jp: 今日は終わりそうもありません。
extensions.en: It doesn't look like finishing today.

extensions.scene: Weather, queues and deadlines are where it lives, and it is the natural thing to say while looking at something that is refusing to improve. It is the natural thing to say while looking at something that is quietly refusing to improve, and the small despair in it is accurate.
extensions.jp: 雨はやみそうにないですね。
extensions.en: The rain doesn't look like stopping.
extensions.t: そうじゃない questions the appearance. そうもない reports that the appearance is of failure. The trap is building the first and meaning the second.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: A conversation has gone slightly wrong and you cannot work out where. You said 違います to something and the other person has become careful with you, and reviewing it later you realise they had not stated a fact at all — they had drawn an inference, and you denied a claim nobody made.
setting.jp: 違います。
setting.en: Wrong — the only no you had, used for four different jobs.

extensions.scene: Japanese separates four denials that English runs together. The fact is false. The inference does not follow. It is not always true. It is not possible at all. Choosing wrong does not sound rude; it sounds confused.
extensions.jp: 嫌いなわけではありません。
extensions.en: It's not that I dislike it — the inference, denied.

extensions.scene: わけではない is the one learners reach for last and the one that rescues most conversations, because most misunderstandings are about what somebody concluded rather than what was said. Most misunderstandings between people are about what somebody concluded rather than about what was actually said, which is why this one earns its place.
extensions.jp: 安いものが悪いとは限りません。
extensions.en: Not always true — the universal denied, the general granted.
extensions.t: Fact 違います · inference わけではない · always とは限らない · possible わけがない · socially barred わけにはいかない.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: You get to the platform as the doors close, and the next one is in forty minutes, and there was a moment twenty minutes ago when you nearly left and did not. The feeling is entirely ordinary and you have no way to say it that does not come out as a flat statement about the past.
setting.jp: 遅く出ました。
setting.en: I left late — a fact, carrying none of it.

extensions.scene: ばよかった puts Step 38's ばいい into the past and turns it into the thing you did not do. The regret is in the grammar, so your voice does not have to do the work.
extensions.jp: もっと早く出ればよかった。
extensions.en: I should have left earlier.

extensions.scene: Aimed at yourself about something you said, it becomes one of the warmest sentences in the language — an apology that never uses the word. Aimed at yourself about something you said, it becomes an apology that never once uses the word for one.
extensions.jp: あんなこと、言わなければよかった。
extensions.en: I shouldn't have said that.
extensions.t: English flips the auxiliary; Japanese flips the VERB. I shouldn't have gone is 行かなければよかった — it would have been good had I not gone.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: Somebody tells you they have an exam tomorrow, or a long flight, or a cold, and there is a thing an English speaker says here without thinking about it at all. You know 頑張ってください and you have used it for everything for a year, and it does not fit any of these.
setting.jp: 頑張ってください。
setting.en: Do your best — which is not what you meant and not always kind.

extensions.scene: といい wishes for something outside anybody's control. It is the piece of daily social glue that has no substitute, and it is how ordinary kindness is expressed between people who are not close.
extensions.jp: 早く良くなるといいですね。
extensions.en: I hope you get better soon.

extensions.scene: The same shape in a question becomes advice-seeking, and which reading is running is decided by the ending rather than the words. Which reading is running is decided by the ending rather than by the words, so the same shape asks and wishes depending on where it stops.
extensions.jp: どうしたらいいですか。
extensions.en: What should I do?
extensions.t: The wish is for what you cannot decide. Hoping for your own action is odd — it addresses the universe about something you control.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: A rumour is going round the office that the department is moving, and nobody knows if it is true. You want to think out loud about what it would mean without being the person who repeated it as fact, and Step 16's たら keeps making it sound like you are planning for it.
setting.jp: 移転したら、大変です。
setting.en: If we move, it'll be a nightmare — as though it were arranged.

extensions.scene: としたら grants a PREMISE for the sake of the argument rather than supposing an event. It reasons from something you are explicitly not asserting, which is precisely the position a rumour puts you in.
extensions.jp: 本当だとしたら、大変です。
extensions.en: If that's true, we've got a problem.

extensions.scene: It is also how any hypothetical discussion gets opened without commitment, from planning meetings to idle speculation over lunch. It opens any hypothetical without committing to it, which is what makes it usable about a rumour you would rather not be caught repeating as fact.
extensions.jp: 一億円もらうとしたら、何をしますか。
extensions.en: Supposing you got a hundred million yen, what would you do?
extensions.t: たら supposes a HAPPENING. としたら supposes a FACT, granted for the argument. Using たら for a premise makes a discussion sound like a plan.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: You are writing to somebody about something that has genuinely affected you, and every sentence you produce is accurate and none of it sounds like it came from a person. 心配しています is true and reads like a status report. You want one sentence that sounds like it came from a person rather than from a form, and everything you own is accurate and cold.
setting.jp: とても心配しています。
setting.en: I'm very worried — accurate, and flat on the page.

extensions.scene: ずにはいられない is the feeling that overrode you: not that you were unable to stop, but that being without doing it was not available. The ず is an old negative that survives for exactly this.
extensions.jp: 心配せずにはいられません。
extensions.en: I can't help worrying.

extensions.scene: It belongs to writing more than speech, which is why it is the right register for a letter and the wrong one for a corridor. It belongs to writing far more than to speech, which is why it is right for a letter and conspicuous in a corridor.
extensions.jp: 言わずにはいられなかった。
extensions.en: I couldn't keep it in.
extensions.t: It is emotionally loud, so a small subject makes it comic. 食べずにはいられない about a biscuit is a joke, usually on purpose.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: Somebody asks when the deadline is and you half-remember it, and the honest state of your knowledge is somewhere below と思います and well above nothing. You say 来週だと思います, and they write it down, and now it is a fact you supplied. You would rather say what you actually know, which is less than a guess and more than nothing, and have it recorded that way.
setting.jp: 来週だと思います。
setting.en: I think it's next week — and it has just become information.

extensions.scene: ような気がする is the weakest claim the language makes, and it announces its own weakness. Below かもしれない and below はず: a sense you cannot back up, marked as one. Below かもしれない and below はず — a sense you cannot back up, and the pattern announces that weakness rather than hiding it.
extensions.jp: 来週のような気がします。
extensions.en: I have a feeling it's next week.

extensions.scene: Which makes it the right shape for raising a half-memory without it being written down, and the wrong shape for anything anybody has to act on. Which makes it right for raising a half-memory and wrong for anything anybody is going to write down and act on.
extensions.jp: どこかで会ったような気がします。
extensions.en: I feel like we've met somewhere before.
extensions.t: It is genuinely weak and will be treated as such — correctly, because you have just said you are guessing.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: You step outside in the middle of October and it is January out there, and the sentence you want is not that it is cold. It is that it is like winter, plainly and impossibly, and 寒いです has nothing in it that carries the disbelief.
setting.jp: とても寒いです。
setting.en: It's very cold — a measurement, not a description.

extensions.scene: まるで sets up a comparison to something you and your listener both know is not the case. Step 15's ようだ alone can read as it seems; まるで in front kills that reading and makes it a figure of speech.
extensions.jp: まるで冬みたいに寒いですね。
extensions.en: It's cold, like winter.

extensions.scene: It is how anything unbelievable gets described — a piece of news, a place, somebody's behaviour — and the frankness is the point: nobody is being fooled. The frankness is the whole point: nobody is being fooled, and the comparison is offered as a figure of speech rather than as a claim about the world.
extensions.jp: まるで夢のようです。
extensions.en: It's like a dream.
extensions.t: まるで almost always needs ようだ or みたいだ to land on. Bare まるで with a plain adjective is incomplete, and it is the standard learner error.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

items.step: Step 40 · Regret, hope, and the unreal

setting.scene: You are trying to write something reflective for the first time — about a decision, and what you hoped, and how it felt — and you find that every tense you own describes things that happened. Nothing you have describes the things that did not.
setting.jp: 行きませんでした。
setting.en: I didn't go — the fact, and none of what surrounds it.

extensions.scene: There are four unrealities here and they are not interchangeable: something you regret not doing, something you hope will happen, a premise granted for argument, and a comparison to something plainly untrue.
extensions.jp: 行けばよかったです。
extensions.en: I should have gone — the regret, with a shape.

extensions.scene: Getting them apart is what makes reflective writing possible at all, and reflective writing is the last register a learner reaches because it is entirely about things not in front of you.
extensions.jp: まるで昨日のことのようです。
extensions.en: It's as though it were yesterday.
extensions.t: Regret ばよかった · wish といい / たらいい · granted premise としたら · frank comparison まるで〜ようだ · unbacked hunch ような気がする.

setting.scene: A child comes back from the park and stops at the door because everybody has stopped talking. There is mud on the shoes, the knees, one sleeve and somehow the back of the neck, and 汚いです covers none of what is actually being looked at, which is quantity rather than quality.
setting.jp: 汚いです。
setting.en: It's dirty — true, and it describes the wrong dimension.

extensions.scene: だらけ says covered in, and the thing it is covered in is always unwelcome. The judgement is inside the word, which is why it needs no adjective around it at all.
extensions.jp: 泥だらけになりましたね。
extensions.en: You've got covered in mud.

extensions.scene: It works as readily on abstract mess as on physical, and it is the standard way a first draft, a form or an excuse gets described. A first draft, a form, an excuse and a room after a party all take it, and in every case the word supplies the sigh so you do not have to.
extensions.jp: この作文は間違いだらけです。
extensions.en: This composition is riddled with mistakes.
extensions.t: Never for good things. 花だらけ about a garden is wrong in a way that is hard to unhear — that is いっぱい.

setting.scene: Two people your age are talking beside you and you are following about half of it, and the half you are losing is not vocabulary — it is a two-syllable ending stuck on the back of ordinary words, over and over, that no textbook you have opened has ever mentioned.
setting.jp: 少し子供みたいです。
setting.en: A bit like a child — correct, and not what they said.

extensions.scene: っぽい is the most productive suffix in casual Japanese and the fastest way to sound like a person rather than a textbook. It means somewhat like, and it clips onto nearly anything.
extensions.jp: ちょっと子供っぽいですね。
extensions.en: That's a bit childish.

extensions.scene: The result behaves as an ordinary い-adjective, so it conjugates the way everything else you know does — which is why it spreads so easily through casual speech. That is why it spreads so easily through casual speech — it costs two syllables and it conjugates like everything else you already know.
extensions.jp: 最近、忘れっぽくなりました。
extensions.en: I've got forgetful lately.
extensions.t: Attached to a person it is almost always mildly unflattering. 大人っぽい is a compliment; 子供っぽい is not, and neither is 安っぽい.

setting.scene: You are reading somebody's account of something that happened to them and one sentence stops you: a verb you know, with an ending you do not, and from the context it plainly means difficult — but you already have にくい for difficult and this is not that word.
setting.jp: 信じにくい話です。
setting.en: A story that's hard to believe — and slightly the wrong kind of hard.

extensions.scene: がたい is difficulty of a different kind: the thing resists being done at all, and the resistance is usually inside you rather than in the object. にくい is awkward; がたい is barely bearable to do.
extensions.jp: 信じがたい話ですね。
extensions.en: That's a hard story to believe.

extensions.scene: It belongs to writing, and it survives in a small fixed set rather than attaching freely — which is the practical difference from にくい and the reason it feels quotational in speech.
extensions.jp: この本は捨てがたいです。
extensions.en: I can't quite bring myself to throw this book out.
extensions.t: You cannot coin new ones. 食べがたい is not a word; 食べにくい is. Learn the set — 信じ, 忘れ, 捨て, 想像し, 理解し, 耐え.

setting.scene: The portion arrives and it is comically large, and the person who brought you here is watching to see whether you like it. You do. You are not going to get through a third of it, and 食べられません says something entirely different and slightly insulting about the food.
setting.jp: 食べられません。
setting.en: I can't eat it — which sounds like there's something wrong with it.

extensions.scene: きれない is about QUANTITY, not ability. Stage 9's きる meant do it all the way through; negated, it says there is more here than can be got through, and the food is blameless.
extensions.jp: 多すぎて、食べきれません。
extensions.en: It's too much — I can't finish it.

extensions.scene: The same shape scales up to anything that defeats an action by sheer volume, and 数えきれないほど is a fixed intensifier you will meet constantly. The same shape scales to anything defeated by sheer volume, and 数えきれないほど is a fixed intensifier you will meet within a week of looking for it.
extensions.jp: 数えきれないほど星があります。
extensions.en: There are more stars than you could count.
extensions.t: 食べられない is inability — allergy, dislike, no teeth. 食べきれない is volume, and it is a compliment to the kitchen.

setting.scene: Somebody you were close to stopped answering after one particular evening, and it has been a year. There is a sentence for this in every language and yours has since — he went out and has not been back since — and Japanese keeps making you say the two halves separately.
setting.jp: 出て行きました。まだ帰りません。
setting.en: He left. He hasn't come back. — two facts, no thread.

extensions.scene: きり ties them into one and puts a hard edge after the last occurrence: that was it, and nothing since. The absence is in the grammar rather than in the second sentence.
extensions.jp: 出て行ったきり、帰ってきません。
extensions.en: He went out and hasn't come back since.

extensions.scene: The same word does an intimate job in its other sense — only these, nobody else — which can be warm or bleak depending entirely on the number. Whether it lands warm or bleak is decided entirely by the number in front of it, and the word itself takes no view on which.
extensions.jp: 二人きりで話したいです。
extensions.en: I'd like to talk with just the two of us.
extensions.t: だけ is neutral only. きり adds that there is nothing and nobody else — 二人きり is intimate, 一人きり is not.

setting.scene: You have had the same conversation about the rent three times this year, and the point is not that it went up. It is that it has only ever gone up, and 高くなりました reports one movement when what you mean is a direction with no sign of turning.
setting.jp: 家賃が高くなりました。
setting.en: The rent went up — one event, and it happened again since.

extensions.scene: 一方だ says the change runs one way and has not stopped. Stage 6's ようになる noted that something changed; this says it is still changing and nothing has turned it. Stage 6's ようになる noted that something changed; this says the change is still running and that nothing so far has turned it around.
extensions.jp: 家賃は上がる一方です。
extensions.en: The rent just keeps going up.

extensions.scene: It attaches only to change verbs, and in practice it attaches to bad ones — which is why a listener hears the pessimism whether or not it was intended. It attaches only to change verbs, and in practice it attaches to unwelcome ones, which is why a listener hears pessimism whether or not you intended any.
extensions.jp: 仕事が増える一方で、休めません。
extensions.en: The work only piles up and I can't take a break.
extensions.t: 良くなる一方だ is grammatical and rare. Speakers reach for this when something is getting worse, and the word has absorbed that.

setting.scene: You read back a paragraph you have written and every sentence is built the same way: a noun, a very, and an adjective. It is correct and it is exhausting, and the Japanese you are reading manages far more precision with far fewer words by hanging something on the end instead.
setting.jp: とても汚い部屋です。
setting.en: A very dirty room — and とても is doing all the work.

extensions.scene: Six suffixes clip onto a word and change what it claims — abundance, approximation, resistance, excess, exclusivity, direction. English does two of these with hyphens and the rest with whole clauses.
extensions.jp: 泥だらけの部屋です。
extensions.en: A room covered in mud — the suffix carries it.

extensions.scene: The gain is not brevity for its own sake. It is that the suffix says which DIMENSION you are talking about, where an adjective plus とても only says how much.
extensions.jp: 安っぽいですが、悪くはありません。
extensions.en: Cheap-looking, though not actually bad.
extensions.t: Four of the six carry a judgement you cannot switch off — だらけ, っぽい, きり, 一方だ. No surrounding politeness cancels it.

setting.scene: You have made something that has to be eaten straight away and the person you made it for is being polite about finishing a phone call. In English you would say while it's hot and the urgency would arrive wrapped in hospitality. 早く食べてください arrives as an instruction.
setting.jp: 早く食べてください。
setting.en: Eat it quickly, please — an order in a kind voice.

extensions.scene: うちに names a window that is closing. The urgency comes from the state expiring rather than from you asking, which is why it hurries somebody without pressing them. The urgency comes from the state expiring rather than from you asking for it, which is what lets you hurry somebody without pressing them at all.
extensions.jp: 熱いうちに召し上がってください。
extensions.en: Please eat it while it's hot.

extensions.scene: The negative form is the commonest and the most useful, because most windows are best described by what has not happened yet. Most windows are best described by what has not happened yet, which is why the negative form is both the commonest and the most useful of the two.
extensions.jp: 忘れないうちにメモします。
extensions.en: I'll note it down before I forget.
extensions.t: Step 19's 間に is a neutral span. うちに says the state is temporary and you should act — 若い間に describes, 若いうちに advises.

setting.scene: A song comes on in a shop and you are somewhere else entirely for four seconds, and it happens with this song every single time without exception. いつも is not right, because いつも is about frequency and this is about reliability — the link has never once failed.
setting.jp: いつも国を思い出します。
setting.en: I always think of home — frequent, but it sounds like a habit.

extensions.scene: たびに is every single occurrence, not merely often. The event and the reaction are welded together, and the pattern says the weld has never broken. The event and the reaction are welded together, and the pattern claims the weld has never once come apart.
extensions.jp: この歌を聞くたびに、国を思い出します。
extensions.en: Every time I hear this song I think of home.

extensions.scene: It wants an occasion with some substance behind it, which is why it belongs to associations and reunions rather than to switches and mechanisms. It wants an occasion with some substance behind it, which is why it belongs to reunions and associations rather than to switches.
extensions.jp: 会うたびに、背が伸びていますね。
extensions.en: You've grown every single time I see you.
extensions.t: Step 16's と chains events mechanically — 押すと開く. たびに is an occasion recurring, and it carries the sense of an event rather than a trigger.

setting.scene: You are going to the post office anyway and your flatmate needs stamps, and you would like to offer without it sounding like a favour that has to be repaid. In English while I'm out does the whole job in four words and removes the debt entirely.
setting.jp: 郵便局に行きます。切手を買いましょうか。
setting.en: I'm going to the post office. Shall I buy stamps? — and now they owe you.

extensions.scene: ついでに makes the second errand a passenger on the first. It tells the other person you are not making a trip for them, which is what removes the obligation. It tells the other person you are not making a trip on their account, and that is precisely what removes the debt from the offer.
extensions.jp: 郵便局に行くついでに、切手を買ってきます。
extensions.en: I'll grab stamps while I'm at the post office.

extensions.scene: It works in the other direction too, and at the front of a request it is the standard way to ask for something small without it landing as an imposition.
extensions.jp: ついでにこれもお願いできますか。
extensions.en: Could you do this too while you're at it?
extensions.t: The main errand must be real and yours. Offering ついでに for a trip made solely for them is transparently kind and literally false.

setting.scene: Somebody who has never left home asks what living abroad is actually like, and every answer you give sounds like a list of facts they could have read. The true answer is that none of it was available to you either until you were standing in it, and that is a claim about knowledge rather than about the place.
setting.jp: 住んで、分かりました。
setting.en: I lived there and understood — two events in a row.

extensions.scene: て初めて says the understanding was not available in advance. It is not one thing then another; it is that the experience was the only route to the knowing. It is not one thing and then another; it is that the experience was the only available route to the knowing, which is a claim about knowledge.
extensions.jp: 住んでみて初めて分かりました。
extensions.en: I didn't really understand until I'd lived there.

extensions.scene: It is close to a default sentence shape for a foreign resident, because almost everything worth saying about the experience has this structure underneath it. Almost everything worth saying about living somewhere unfamiliar has this structure underneath it, which is why it becomes a default shape.
extensions.jp: 失って初めて、大切さに気づきます。
extensions.en: You only realise the value once it's gone.
extensions.t: It needs a realisation on the other side — 分かる, 気づく. An ordinary next event makes it the wrong pattern.

setting.scene: You have to write two lines telling people what the meeting decided, and から and ので both put the reason in front, which makes the decision arrive as an afterthought at the end of a long sentence nobody has read to the bottom of. Nobody reads to the bottom of a long sentence, and the decision is the only part of it anybody needed.
setting.jp: よく話し合ったので、こうなりました。
setting.en: We discussed it, so this is what happened — the outcome buried at the end.

extensions.scene: た結果 reports the outcome of a deliberate process and puts the weight on the outcome. It is the register of minutes, reports and news, where what was decided matters more than the discussing.
extensions.jp: よく話し合った結果、こうなりました。
extensions.en: After a full discussion, this is where we landed.

extensions.scene: その結果 stands alone at the head of the next sentence, which is how a written account moves from what was done to what came of it without a long joining clause.
extensions.jp: その結果、参加者が増えました。
extensions.en: As a result, attendance rose.
extensions.t: The cause must be an EFFORT. 雨が降った結果 is odd — nobody conducted the rain. 調べた結果 and 相談した結果 are natural.

setting.scene: The board at the station says the trains are delayed and gives a reason in four characters and a particle, and you read it as a purpose — trains delayed in order to have an accident — and stand there for a second genuinely confused before the sense rearranges itself.
setting.jp: 事故がありました。電車が遅れています。
setting.en: There was an accident. Trains are delayed. — two sentences, unlinked.

extensions.scene: ために joins them, and which of its two jobs is running depends on whether the thing named is something anybody CHOSE. Nobody chose the accident, so it reads as a cause.
extensions.jp: 事故のため、電車が遅れています。
extensions.en: Trains are delayed because of an accident.

extensions.scene: Put a volitional verb in the same slot and the identical shape becomes a purpose, which is the sense you already half-know from everyday speech. The identical shape has become a purpose, and nothing marks the switch except whether the thing named was something somebody chose.
extensions.jp: 日本語を勉強するために来ました。
extensions.en: I came in order to study Japanese.
extensions.t: Step 6's ように covers purposes you cannot control — 分かるように. ために needs a purpose you can aim at: 上手になるように, not ために.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You have four ways to say while and you have been choosing between them by feel, and today somebody answered a question you had not asked — you said 間に where you meant うちに and they heard a description where you intended advice. You have been choosing between them by feel for months, and today the feel was wrong in a way somebody noticed.
setting.jp: 若い間に旅行しました。
setting.en: I travelled while I was young — a description of when.

extensions.scene: The time system is nearly complete now and the distinctions are fine. A neutral span. A closing window. A reliable recurrence. An errand carried along. A realisation that needed the doing.
extensions.jp: 若いうちに旅行したほうがいいですよ。
extensions.en: Travel while you're young — the window is closing.

extensions.scene: English uses while for the first three of those, which is exactly why they have to be sorted deliberately rather than picked up by exposure. English uses while for three of these, which is exactly why they have to be sorted deliberately rather than absorbed by exposure.
extensions.jp: 会うたびに大きくなりますね。
extensions.en: Every single time — not merely often.
extensions.t: Span 間に · closing window うちに · every occurrence たびに · piggybacked errand ついでに · only after doing て初めて.

setting.scene: Somebody has been explaining something to you for two minutes and has been kind about it, and you have understood roughly seventy per cent and are about to nod. If you nod you will act on the seventy and find out later which thirty mattered.
setting.jp: はい、分かりました。
setting.en: Yes, I understand — and you are about to find out that you don't.

extensions.scene: つまり lets you say it back, shorter, and find out whether you had it. It is the single most useful word in the room for a learner, because it converts a nod into a check.
extensions.jp: つまり、明日は休みということですか。
extensions.en: So what you mean is tomorrow's a day off?

extensions.scene: It pairs naturally with Step 35's ということ, which is what makes the restatement sound like a summary rather than a doubt about their explanation. It converts a nod into a check, and the cost of not checking is finding out later which thirty per cent was the part that mattered.
extensions.jp: つまり、そういうことです。
extensions.en: That, in short, is the situation.
extensions.t: What follows must be SHORTER and no newer. A fresh point after つまり confuses badly, because a compression was expected.

setting.scene: You are telling a story at dinner and it has a turn in it — you did everything right and it went wrong anyway — and でも flattens the turn into an ordinary contrast, so the table is politely waiting for a point that has already gone past.
setting.jp: 早く出ました。でも、間に合いませんでした。
setting.en: I left early. But I didn't make it. — flat, and the surprise is lost.

extensions.scene: ところが is the but that says an expectation broke. It tells the listener that what follows overturned something the speaker actually believed, which is what makes a story a story.
extensions.jp: 早く出ました。ところが、間に合いませんでした。
extensions.en: I left early. And yet I still didn't make it.

extensions.scene: It is the hinge of almost every anecdote told out loud in Japanese, and hearing it is a signal to wait — the interesting half has not arrived yet. Hearing it is a signal to wait, because the interesting half of whatever is being told has not arrived yet.
extensions.jp: ところが、誰も来なかったんです。
extensions.en: But then — nobody came.
extensions.t: It cannot join clauses inside one sentence; that is が or けど. And it needs a genuine reversal, not an ordinary contrast.

setting.scene: You are asked whether the city is a good place to live and the honest answer is both things at once — it is easier than home in three ways and lonelier in one — and every connector you own makes the second half cancel the first.
setting.jp: 便利です。でも、寂しいです。
setting.en: It's convenient. But it's lonely. — and the but wins.

extensions.scene: 一方で holds both as true rather than letting one defeat the other. Both halves describe the same subject, and the pattern is what makes a judgement read as considered instead of one-sided.
extensions.jp: 便利な一方で、少し寂しいです。
extensions.en: Convenient, and on the other hand a little lonely.

extensions.scene: It is the backbone of any writing that weighs something up, and it is the difference between an opinion and an argument on the page. Both halves have to describe the same subject; that is what separates it from ordinary contrast and what makes a judgement read as considered.
extensions.jp: 父は厳しい一方で、優しいところもあります。
extensions.en: My father is strict, and yet he has a kind side too.
extensions.t: Not Step 41's 一方だ, which is a one-way change and means nearly the opposite. 増える一方だ is only ever up; 増える一方で holds two truths.

setting.scene: You are writing three sentences arguing for something and every one of them front-loads the reason, so the position you actually hold does not appear until halfway down and the reader has been holding a clause open the whole time without knowing what for. The reader has been holding an unfinished clause open the whole time without yet knowing what it was for.
setting.jp: 時間がないから、反対です。
setting.en: Since there's no time, I'm against it — the position arrives last.

extensions.scene: なぜなら lets you state the position first and justify it afterwards, which is the order an argument wants and the opposite of the order から forces. The reader is no longer holding an open clause waiting to find out what it was for, which is the whole reason the order matters.
extensions.jp: 私は反対です。なぜなら、時間がないからです。
extensions.en: I'm against it. The reason is that there isn't time.

extensions.scene: The opening and the closing are a pair — からです is not optional in careful writing, and dropping it leaves the sentence audibly unfinished. The opening and the closing are a pair, and dropping からです leaves the sentence audibly unfinished to anybody reading carefully.
extensions.jp: なぜかというと、経験がないからです。
extensions.en: The reason is that I have no experience.
extensions.t: In speech it is stiff. Spoken Japanese uses だって or just から; なぜなら at a dinner table sounds like reading from a report.

setting.scene: Somebody looks at something you made on your first attempt and says a sentence with a shape in it you have not met, and you catch that it was positive and miss that it was also, very gently, a measurement against what a first attempt is expected to be.
setting.jp: 上手ですね。
setting.en: That's good — a compliment with no reference point.

extensions.scene: にしては judges a thing against the standard for its own category and marks a departure from it. The praise and the limit arrive in the same breath, exactly as English does with for a.
extensions.jp: 初めてにしては、よくできました。
extensions.en: For a first attempt, that went well.

extensions.scene: It is everywhere in feedback and in weather and in prices, and a learner hears it about their own Japanese more often than about anything else. A learner hears it about their own Japanese more often than about anything else, usually kindly and always with the measurement attached.
extensions.jp: 冬にしては暖かいですね。
extensions.en: It's warm for winter.
extensions.t: It always contains a small put-down. Check which category you have placed the person in before you say it — the frame is doing that work.

setting.scene: You are annoyed with somebody and they have a reason, and the reason is real. You do not want to reject it, because it is true, and you also do not want to let it settle the matter, because a message would have taken four seconds.
setting.jp: 忙しかったですね。
setting.en: You were busy — granted, and now the conversation is over.

extensions.scene: にしても grants the point and presses on anyway. It is how an adult disagreement is conducted in Japanese: concede first, in the grammar, and the objection lands as reasonable rather than as a refusal to listen.
extensions.jp: 忙しいにしても、連絡はできたはずです。
extensions.en: Busy or not, you could have got in touch.

extensions.scene: Doubled, it covers both branches at once, which is the standard way to force a decision without arguing for either side of it. It forces a decision without arguing for either branch, which is why it turns up whenever something has been left undecided too long.
extensions.jp: 行くにしても行かないにしても、早く決めて。
extensions.en: Going or not, decide soon.
extensions.t: One kana from にしては and easy to mishear. にしては measures against a standard; にしても grants and overrides.

setting.scene: You want to ask a favour that is genuinely a favour, and you have something to offer back, and Japanese so far has given you no way to put the two halves in one sentence — so the offer arrives afterwards and sounds like an apology for having asked.
setting.jp: 手伝ってください。あとで夕食をおごります。
setting.en: Please help. I'll buy dinner later. — a request, then a consolation.

extensions.scene: 代わりに puts the trade in one sentence and makes it an exchange rather than a request with compensation attached. The other person can accept the whole thing at once. The other person can accept or decline the whole thing at once, rather than accepting a favour and then discovering there was a price attached.
extensions.jp: 手伝う代わりに、夕食をおごりますよ。
extensions.en: I'll buy you dinner in return for the help.

extensions.scene: The same word covers plain substitution, which is its commoner and more everyday job — the ingredient you did not have, the plan that changed. It is the commoner of its two jobs by a wide margin, and the one you will produce without thinking about it within a week.
extensions.jp: バターの代わりに油を使いました。
extensions.en: I used oil instead of butter.
extensions.t: Step 37's にかわって is taking somebody's ROLE. 代わりに is the ordinary instead of, and it works on objects and actions too.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You finish a piece of writing and every sentence in it is correct, and read together they are a list. Somebody Japanese reads it and says it is very clear, in the tone that means something is missing, and what is missing is any signal of how the sentences are supposed to relate.
setting.jp: 便利です。寂しいです。反対です。
setting.en: Convenient. Lonely. I'm against it. — three correct sentences, no argument.

extensions.scene: Japanese puts its joints at the HEAD of a sentence rather than between clauses, which is why learner writing so often reads as a list: the joints were never learned, only the clause-joiners が and から.
extensions.jp: 便利な一方で、寂しいです。だから、反対です。
extensions.en: Convenient, and on the other hand lonely. So I'm against it.

extensions.scene: Six joints cover most of what a paragraph needs to do, and having them is the difference between passing a writing task and being read to the end of it.
extensions.jp: 安いと思いました。ところが、高かったです。
extensions.en: I thought it'd be cheap. It wasn't.
extensions.t: Restate つまり · reverse ところが · balance 一方で · justify なぜなら〜からです · add それに · conclude その結果.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 10 is written register throughout and necessarily uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT. Furigana needed across this stage — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You are near the end of a reading passage and doing well, and then a sentence has べきではありません in it and you stall — not because it is hard, but because you have only ever met べき in its positive form and your eye refuses to accept that the negative is simply the negative. You lose thirty seconds to a word you already know.
setting.jp: そうするべきです。
setting.en: You should do that — the only half you were taught.

extensions.scene: It negates exactly the way everything else does, and the moment you see that, the second half of the pattern costs nothing. Most of what is left on any list at this level is this: forms you can already build, that nobody happened to point at while you were learning the first half of them.
extensions.jp: そうするべきではありません。
extensions.en: You shouldn't do that.

extensions.scene: The same is true of ばかりでなく and だけでなく, which are ばかり and だけ with a not only bolted on, and of たとえ〜ても and どんなに〜ても, which are Step 21's ても with an adverb in front telling you how far the concession stretches before it gives.
extensions.jp: 安いだけでなく、質もいいです。
extensions.en: Not only cheap — the quality's good too.
extensions.t: The sibling forms carry no new machinery. The reason to gather them in one place is that meeting them one at a time makes each look like a fresh pattern to memorise, when the whole set is five minutes of work.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You have asked a colleague whether they could help with something on Saturday. They breathe in slightly, tilt their head, and say four words — and then stop. You wait, because in English a sentence that stops there has not finished, and the silence runs long enough that you start asking the question again.
setting.jp: 土曜日、手伝ってもらえますか。
setting.en: Could you help on Saturday? — the question you asked.

extensions.scene: The sentence was finished. ちょっと and a trailing pause is a complete refusal, and it is complete precisely because ending it would force the word out. Say it back yourself and you have declined without once being unkind to anybody.
extensions.jp: 土曜日はちょっと…
extensions.en: Saturday's a bit — a whole sentence, in Japanese.

extensions.scene: This step's わけではない does the harder version: denying the conclusion somebody has drawn while leaving everything they actually said standing, which is what you need when a flat no would simply be false.
extensions.jp: 行きたくないわけではないんです。
extensions.en: It's not that I don't want to go.
extensions.t: The refusal is built to protect the ASKER — if the no is never said, nobody is on record as having been turned down. And the reverse is the half learners miss: 難しいですね about your proposal IS the answer.

claims: In ordinary Japanese, いいえ answers questions of fact rather than declining offers, refusing requests or disagreeing with opinions; those are typically carried by a trailing ちょっと, by 難しい, by 考えておきます, or by patterns that deny an inference rather than a statement.
Directness varies substantially by individual, region, industry and age, and has been increasing among younger speakers and in internationally-facing workplaces.
flags: ⚠️ HIGHEST-RISK LESSON IN THE APP OUTSIDE THE KEIGO STAGE. It makes claims about how Japanese speakers decline things, which is the single most stereotyped topic in the field. It is deliberately written about REGISTER AND MARKERS rather than national character, and it argues against the stereotype in the text — but whether the framing lands is a judgement only a native reader can make. Read this one first.

No citable source: these are observations about conversational practice rather than statistics. Stated as practice, with the variation caveat in the lesson body, rather than asserted as a fact about Japan.
Stage 9/10 culture lessons necessarily use kanji outside KANJI_DICT (回覧板・年賀状・仕方・訪米 and the like). Furigana needed — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: Somebody knocks about three weeks after you move in. A neighbour you have not met hands you a flat plastic folder with a grid of names printed down the front, says one short sentence, and goes. Inside is a single sheet about refuse collection. Your name is third from the top, with an empty box beside it, and you have no idea whether that box means read, agreed, or paid.
setting.jp: 回覧板が回ってきました。
setting.en: The circulating folder has come round.

extensions.scene: The box means read. Tick it or stamp it and carry the folder to the next house on the grid — that is the entire obligation, and the common first-year embarrassment is the folder sitting on your table for a week while eleven households wait behind you.
extensions.jp: 次の家に持って行きます。
extensions.en: I'll take it on to the next house.

extensions.scene: And the sheet inside it is this step's grammar in the wild. Every heading on a neighbourhood notice hangs a noun off a claim with one of these six particles, and none of them has a verb in it at all.
extensions.jp: ゴミの分別についてのお知らせ
extensions.en: Notice concerning refuse separation.
extensions.t: Tokyo's metropolitan government now subsidises 町会・自治会 moving to 電子回覧板, and wards including Minato run their own. Paper persists anyway: the volunteers who run a 町内会 skew elderly, so most areas that digitise end up running both.

claims: A 回覧板 is a physical folder circulated house to house by a neighbourhood association, with a grid of household names to be stamped or ticked and passed on.
The Tokyo Metropolitan Government operates a subsidy for neighbourhood associations adopting 電子回覧板 and digital fee collection (announced April 2026); Minato Ward runs its own digital 回覧板 scheme.
Digitisation is commonly run in parallel with paper because association membership skews elderly, which increases rather than reduces the administrative burden.
sources: 東京都 · 町会・自治会の電子回覧板や町会費のデジタル化を応援 (April 2026) — https://www.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/information/press/2026/04/2026040810
港区 · デジタル回覧板 — https://www.city.minato.tokyo.jp/kuminkyoudoutan/digital_kairannbann.html
札幌市 · 町内会における回覧板のデジタル化について — https://www4.city.sapporo.jp/scg/task/post-005.html

setting.scene: You buy a manga because somebody said it was easy, and you get four pages in before admitting that you can read every kanji on the page and still not know what is happening. The verbs are the problem. You know 言う and you know かける, and 言いかけた is not obviously either of them, and there are six more like it before the chapter ends.
setting.jp: 彼は何か言いました。
setting.en: He said something — the sentence you can build.

extensions.scene: This step is the join. A compound verb welds a second verb onto the first to add a direction, a completeness or an attitude, and once you can see the seam the vocabulary stops being six hundred new words and becomes two hundred you already had.
extensions.jp: 彼は何か言いかけて、やめました。
extensions.en: He started to say something and stopped.

extensions.scene: Which makes this roughly the point where reading for pleasure stops being a punishment — and manga aimed at younger readers prints furigana over the kanji, so the reading is handed to you and only the meaning is your problem.
extensions.jp: 駅前で先生を見かけました。
extensions.en: I happened to spot my teacher outside the station.
extensions.t: ⚠️ Manga dialogue is stylised. 俺様, わし, ですわ mark a character as a type, and a learner who absorbs them unnoticed will sound like a cartoon. Read it for the verbs and the rhythm; take your register from people.

claims: Manga aimed at younger readerships (少年・少女 lines) commonly prints furigana over kanji, while lines aimed at adult readerships (青年・女性) frequently do not.
Manga dialogue uses role-marking pronouns and sentence-endings that are stylised rather than typical of ordinary speech.
flags: The furigana claim is a general publishing convention rather than a universal rule, and is stated as commonly rather than always. A reviewer should confirm the 少年/青年 split is fair as put.
Stage 9/10 culture lessons necessarily use kanji outside KANJI_DICT (回覧板・年賀状・仕方・訪米 and the like). Furigana needed — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You have said おかげさまで perhaps two hundred times, because somebody taught it to you in week three as the answer to how are you. Today somebody asks what it means and you find you have no idea — you know when to say it and you have never once known what is inside it.
setting.jp: おかげさまで、元気です。
setting.en: I'm well, thanks — said for a year without being parsed.

extensions.scene: It is Stage 9's おかげで, frozen, with an honorific さま in it: thanks to you. And there is no connection whatever between the person asking and your health. The phrase hands somebody credit for nothing in particular, which is a courteous thing to do and a strange one to explain.
extensions.jp: おかげで、間に合いました。
extensions.en: Thanks to you, I made it — the live version of the same word.

extensions.scene: The whole set works this way. お疲れさまです is literally you must be tired and functionally hello, goodbye and well done; 失礼します is literally I commit a rudeness and works on at least four different doors.
extensions.jp: お先に失礼します。
extensions.en: Excuse me for leaving ahead of you.
extensions.t: ⚠️ ご苦労さまです means nearly the same as お疲れさま and points DOWNWARD, from a superior to a subordinate. A learner who uses it on their boss has made a real mistake in a friendly voice.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
Stage 9/10 culture lessons necessarily use kanji outside KANJI_DICT (回覧板・年賀状・仕方・訪米 and the like). Furigana needed — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: You decide you are ready to read a news site, and the first headline defeats you in a way that feels unfair: eight kanji, one comma, and no verb anywhere in it. You look for the particles that would tell you what relates to what and there are none of those either, and the article underneath is perfectly readable.
setting.jp: 首相は来月アメリカに行きます。
setting.en: The PM will visit America next month — the sentence you'd build.

extensions.scene: A headline is a different grammar. The verb goes, the particles go, a comma does は's job, and a single へ carries the entire future tense. Once you expect that, the density stops being an obstacle and becomes the reason headlines are fast to read.
extensions.jp: 首相、来月訪米へ
extensions.en: PM to visit the US next month.

extensions.scene: And the body of the article is this step, at full length. Name the source, then report — which is why a headline is the highest-density place these relations ever appear.
extensions.jp: 調査によると、去年に比べて３割減
extensions.en: Per the survey: down thirty per cent on last year.
extensions.t: か marks the unconfirmed (値上げか — a price rise?), と carries findings and quotes, and proportions come in 割, tenths, far more readily than in percentages. NHK's NEWS WEB EASY uses the same conventions with furigana.

claims: Japanese newspaper headlines routinely omit verbs and particles, use へ to mark a forthcoming event, use か to mark an unconfirmed report, and express proportions in 割.
NHK publishes NEWS WEB EASY, a simplified news service with furigana intended for children and language learners.
flags: Headline conventions are stated from the form itself and are readily checkable against any Japanese news front page; a reviewer should confirm the へ and か characterisations are put fairly.
Stage 9/10 culture lessons necessarily use kanji outside KANJI_DICT (回覧板・年賀状・仕方・訪米 and the like). Furigana needed — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: The line is down, the replacement bus is an hour away, and the person beside you has said the same four syllables three times in five minutes. You have read that this phrase reveals something deep about Japanese fatalism, and standing on a wet platform it does not feel like a philosophy — it feels like something to say when there is nothing to say.
setting.jp: 電車が止まりました。
setting.en: The train has stopped — the fact, and nothing else.

extensions.scene: 仕方がない is this step's しかない from the other side: しかない says there is only this option, 仕方がない says there is none. Both close a decision, and neither one complains. In practice the phrase is doing an ordinary job — it ends a circling conversation nobody can fix.
extensions.jp: 仕方がないですね。
extensions.en: Nothing to be done — and the subject is now closed.

extensions.scene: Its other job is kinder and less written about. Said to somebody blaming themselves, しょうがないよ means it was not your fault and nobody could have done differently — which is absolution rather than resignation.
extensions.jp: しょうがないよ、誰も分からなかったんだから。
extensions.en: It's not on you — nobody could have known.
extensions.t: ⚠️ Because it closes a topic, using it about somebody ELSE's serious misfortune can read as filing their problem away. About your own troubles it is unremarkable; about theirs it has to be offered as comfort, not as a verdict.

claims: 仕方がない / しょうがない functions conversationally to close a topic that cannot be resolved, and also to absolve somebody who is blaming themselves.
The common claim that the phrase evidences a distinctively Japanese fatalism is contested, and the lesson presents it as contested rather than settled.
flags: ⚠️ SECOND-HIGHEST RISK in this batch. It engages directly with a well-known cultural generalisation about Japan. Handled in the cc-baito shape — the received reading is stated AS a received reading and the narrower defensible claim is stated separately — but a reviewer should say whether the balance is right.
Stage 9/10 culture lessons necessarily use kanji outside KANJI_DICT (回覧板・年賀状・仕方・訪米 and the like). Furigana needed — flagged once per lesson rather than per line.

setting.scene: It is the fourth of January and three cards have arrived from people you work with, all of them delivered on the first, and you sent nothing because nobody told you there was a deadline in December for post that arrives in January. There is a repair for this and you do not know it either.
setting.jp: 年賀状をもらいました。
setting.en: I received New Year cards — and sent none.

extensions.scene: The cards are posted in December, held by the post office, and delivered together on the first. There is a cut-off around the twenty-fifth for guaranteed first-of-January delivery, and hitting it is the whole game. Miss it and the repair is 寒中見舞い, sent after the seventh.
extensions.jp: 忘れないうちに、年賀状を出します。
extensions.en: I'll post the cards before I forget.

extensions.scene: This step's grammar is the point: every obligation in the Japanese year is an OCCASION rather than a date. たびに for what recurs, うちに for a window closing, ついでに for the errand folded into a trip you were making anyway.
extensions.jp: 帰省のついでに、お墓参りをしました。
extensions.en: I visited the grave while I was back home anyway.
extensions.t: The custom is collapsing fast enough to watch. Japan Post's initial run for the 2026 cards was about 748 million — down 30.1 per cent year on year, the largest fall on record and the fifteenth consecutive annual decline, against a 2004 peak near 4.46 billion. So do not assume you are expected to send them: ask.

claims: Japan Post's initial print run for 2026 New Year cards was approximately 748 million, a fall of about 30.1 per cent on the previous year — the largest recorded fall and the fifteenth consecutive annual decline.
The peak was approximately 4.46 billion cards for 2004, making the 2026 figure roughly one sixth of it.
Commonly cited causes are the spread of messaging apps and the October 2024 increase in postal charges.
New Year cards posted by a late-December cut-off are held and delivered together on 1 January; 寒中見舞い sent after 7 January is the customary repair for a missed card.
sources: 時事ドットコム · 来年の年賀はがき、３割減 発行枚数、過去最大の減少幅―日本郵便 (29 Aug 2025) — https://www.jiji.com/jc/article?k=2025082900750&g=eco
時事ドットコム · 年賀状の受け付け開始 発行枚数は３割減―日本郵便 (15 Dec 2025) — https://www.jiji.com/jc/article?k=2025121500126&g=soc
不破雷蔵 · 2026年用の当初発行枚数は7億4841万枚…年賀はがきの発行枚数などの実情 (Yahoo!ニュース エキスパート) — https://news.yahoo.co.jp/expert/articles/f9529f54e1bd10616039f10a00ddb8d9d960c895
